item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-zhixing-十年攒钱不舍得买车-直到妈妈确诊癌症才懂延迟满足有前提/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-zhixing-十年攒钱不舍得买车-直到妈妈确诊癌症才懂延迟满足有前提/
item.description: He spent a decade saving for a Tesla, repeatedly redirecting funds to real estate and stocks; his mother's pancreatic cancer diagnosis—where a breakthrough targeted drug extends life by only 8 to 9 months—taught him that delayed gratification requires a prerequisite: you must live to enjoy the payoff.
item.content:encoded:
He spent a decade saving for a Tesla, repeatedly redirecting funds to real estate and stocks; his mother's pancreatic cancer diagnosis—where a breakthrough targeted drug extends life by only 8 to 9 months—taught him that delayed gratification requires a prerequisite: you must live to enjoy the payoff.

Five listeners face spending dilemmas, but Junyan's story hits hardest: ten years of deferred reward crashing into his mother's cancer diagnosis.

10:12 Major life transitions have no fixed timeline; settling becomes your life
Ayu bought a transition apartment at 21 with parental help, expecting to leave within a decade. Instead she stayed indefinitely, never replacing inherited furniture and appliances from the previous owner. She slowly realized that major life transitions—marriage, new status—have no predetermined timeline. Days simply accumulate until you recognize you're living permanently in what was supposed to be temporary. That recognition pushed her to finally invest 5,000+ yuan in a new armchair.

27:25 This trip is a gift you're giving yourself, not your parents
Mumu has wanted to take his parents and younger brother on a trip to Beijing and Shanghai for two or three years but hasn't dared mention it. He's explicit about his motive: this isn't a gift to thank them, it's a gift to himself. He wants them to perform the role of perfect parents in a harmonious family, replacing childhood memories of his parents fighting, throwing dishes, breaking things. He thinks perhaps a faint hint of love exists somewhere in the family; the trip is meant to amplify it.

37:33 He calculated a 70 per cent probability the family would fight about money
Mumu's worst-case scenario is a public family argument at a tourist site, with his parents accusing him and his brother of wasteful spending and calling relatives to complain. He's assigned this outcome a 70 per cent probability. His father wants the money reserved for his brother's wedding; his mother wants him to fund a rural house renovation that no one will ever occupy. Mumu has already paid for home renovations and his brother's tuition and rent. Yet he hasn't abandoned the idea—just scaled it to a modest New Year trip to nearby cities.

58:46 A single sentence in a college politics class ended six years of score anxiety
Xiaobai built self-confidence through test scores in middle and high school. In a college politics class, his teacher posed a question that struck him: ‘You worked so hard to get into a 985 university—is it just so you can sell yourself at a better price in the job market?’ The question cracked his score-based self-esteem. He spent years reading heavily to escape what he calls his ‘existential crisis’, and in the process gained new insight into why Apple built such an addictive brand.

1:28:05 Running short on budget for a bracelet turned into an unexpected gift
Daisy quit her job at a top-tier hospital and spent three years preparing for the US medical licensing exam. She wanted to buy a Van Cleef & Arpels red five-leaf clover bracelet to mark the end of her days in sterile gloves. But unemployment left her anxious; she hesitated and even researched crystal alternatives. Her laptop broke during the 11.11 sales event, consuming her budget. She met with her graduate advisor to talk through her anxiety—the advisor, knowing nothing of the bracelet, casually gave her an amber bracelet and said: ‘There's no setback in life you can't survive, and nothing you lose that you can't bear.’

1:42:17 He spends freely on family happiness but treats his own emotional needs as worthless
Junyan's consumer rule is simple: first decide if something is an investment or a consumption expense. If it's consumption, reject it. That's why the Tesla never happened. But the rule doesn't apply to others. Whenever family members want a new phone, he satisfies the request immediately. He flies economy, uses an iPhone11 Pro. When asked why, he can't explain it. He just believes he cannot measure the emotional value he brings to people around him, so his own emotional value has never felt worth serious consideration.

1:50:23 Delayed gratification only works if you're sure you'll live to enjoy the payoff
Junyan wanted to buy a Tesla a decade ago. He invested the money he earned in university into Tesla stock, which grew 8 to 9 times, then moved all of it into Australian real estate. The car was never bought. Two years ago, his mother was diagnosed with mid-stage pancreatic cancer. Only about 20 per cent of pancreatic cancer patients are eligible for surgery. The first breakthrough targeted drug ever discovered for this disease extends life by an average of 8 to 9 months. That diagnosis taught him something new about the principle he'd lived by for years: delayed gratification has a prerequisite. You must first be certain you have a future.

item.title: Black October rewrites security's rules: AI attacks end-to-end in 20 minutes
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-a16z-黑色十月改变安全规则-ai-攻击全程只要-20-分钟/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-a16z-黑色十月改变安全规则-ai-攻击全程只要-20-分钟/
item.description: Wiz's CTO calls it a black-swan event: open-source models have caught up with closed-source models' vulnerability-discovery ability, and attackers can now go from initial access to stealing all keys in about 20 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Wiz's CTO calls it a black-swan event: open-source models have caught up with closed-source models' vulnerability-discovery ability, and attackers can now go from initial access to stealing all keys in about 20 minutes.

Reveals the new reality facing security executives and founders: not whether to invest in security, but how to design systems assuming they will be breached. Information-dense with virtually no filler.

2:05 Black October represents a black swan in security history
Ami calls this October a black swan because he has never seen so many security incidents occur simultaneously in a single month. This includes both surging numbers and severity of vulnerabilities discovered—including what he believes may be the most serious PHP vulnerability ever found by AI—and AI attackers targeting companies, startups, and connected devices like refrigerators at scale with unprecedented speed and sophistication. He emphasizes this is not theoretical; it is happening now.

4:09 Open-source models are closing the gap faster than anyone predicted
A few months ago, the team estimated open-source models lagged closed-source models by several months. That gap is now closing rapidly. Attacks are no longer limited to complex PHP vulnerabilities; even simple API mistakes can now be found and exploited. Attackers can now complete the entire chain—from finding a zero-day through running code in a customer environment to finishing the breach—in about 20 minutes, work that once took top attackers weeks or months.

5:37 Every AI platform becomes a target for attackers seeking the keys
Wiz's blog initially listed nine AI development platform companies attacked in October. That number grew daily and had reached 915 by recording time. These companies are targeted specifically because they hold AI keys. Attackers do not need advanced skill—only the ability to use open-source models capable of finding code problems, then convert those findings into actual breaches within 20 minutes.

7:13 PHP patches arrive quickly, but coverage will remain incomplete for years
PHP comprises about 70% of externally accessible technology, affecting nearly all customer environments. The positive: customers respond fast, with about 50% completing patches within the first two to three days. The negative: because the base is 70% of the internet, full remediation of this single vulnerability will take years. Many old PHP versions will never receive patches, creating permanent gaps.

8:15 Exploit code can be written and leaked faster than patches deployed
Ami identifies a structural misalignment: AI has dramatically compressed the time to write working exploit code, but patch deployment time has not shortened; over the past 20-30 years it has actually lengthened. Moreover, information often leaks before CVE publication. Even in PHP's case, where the team coordinated with officials for months, disclosure came early. Customers had no time to wait for patches. The only realistic path forward, Ami argues, is for new companies to integrate automated development, testing, and CI/CD from day one—enabling them to instruct the system to ‘fix this’ and have it complete automatically. Established companies rarely manage this.

15:37 Security teams must route alerts to the right model for each case
Ami uses Blue Agent as an example: running the most expensive model on every alert is impossible, so you design a pipeline—deterministic detection first, then a cheap model, then the most expensive model for final judgment on suspected threats. He argues this layered, cost-efficient multi-model pipeline design is the real engineering challenge facing security companies (and all AI systems companies). Otherwise, code scanning alone could consume millions in budget without solving the continuous problem.

21:41 The highest ROI is continuous scanning of exposed surfaces, not code alone
Ami is direct: Mythos-style code scanning generates the most press, but he argues it is not the most efficient approach. The real priority for continuous scanning is unauthenticated surfaces directly exposed to the internet—where actual attackers actually start. Two days before recording, a major breach occurred because hardcoded keys in a mobile app led to mass user data theft. That is the actual entry point. He advocates continuous self-attack simulation using a Red Agent, because systems secure today may become vulnerable tomorrow as new model capabilities emerge.

35:11 Most of what security teams do is not actually security work
Ami makes a sharp observation: security teams devote substantial time to compliance reports and administrative tasks, with only a small fraction on red-team testing, risk mitigation, and incident preparation. He argues that security work consists truly of only two categories—preparing for attacks through self-attack testing, and installing guardrails against breaches through detection and response. Everything else should be eliminated. Budget and effort should concentrate on finding and handling critical risks, not buying more tools or working through compliance checklists.

item.title: Bedtime bargaining, screens, overstimulation: five sleep-blocking habits
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-raisinggh-睡前谈判-开着电视-太兴奋-五个让孩子更难入睡的习惯/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-raisinggh-睡前谈判-开着电视-太兴奋-五个让孩子更难入睡的习惯/
item.description: Sleep resistance is a biological response, not defiance. What genuinely undermines sleep is parental-created stimulation before bed, inconsistent routines, screens, negotiating bedtime, and environmental problems.
item.content:encoded:
Sleep resistance is a biological response, not defiance. What genuinely undermines sleep is parental-created stimulation before bed, inconsistent routines, screens, negotiating bedtime, and environmental problems.

Concrete, actionable bedtime habits with no complex theory—direct to practice. High repetition makes one listen enough to capture the essentials.

2:04 Children's sleep resistance is biology and psychology, never rebellion
Even tired kids resist sleep—this is biological and psychological, not intentional defiance. Melatonin doesn't switch on instantly; the pre-sleep window is crucial. Cortisol and overstimulation delay sleep by 20 to 45 minutes. Parents often frame sleep problems as discipline issues and vice versa. Younger children lack self-regulation from excitement and need parents to actively calm them.

4:10 Your sleep anxiety transmits to your child
A meta-analysis found significant, consistent links between caregiver-perceived stress and worse child sleep: shorter duration, more night waking, more pre-sleep resistance. The more parents anxiously fixate on "must sleep now," even silently, the more kids absorb that pressure. Advice: remind yourself this isn't an emergency. Settle your own internal story first, then handle the child's sleep.

6:12 Disrupted bedtime routines keep children neurologically hypervigilant
Research shows bedtime sequence matters more than most parents realize. Random order keeps the nervous system on high alert; repeating the same 3-4 steps nightly, consistently across settings, helps more. Meanwhile, guilt-driven or anxiety-driven compliance with child requests (staying in the room, repeated soothing, extra water, co-sleeping from worry) directly correlates with worse sleep problems. Higher compliance, worse outcomes—a vicious cycle.

10:25 Pre-sleep screens are like pre-sleep espresso
TV or iPad at bedtime equals a shot of espresso, then confusion about poor sleep. It's not just blue light; it's screen content excitement and rapid-fire information. Face-level tablets are worse than wall-mounted TVs. Fix: zero screens in the final hour before bed. Even if kids fall asleep fine, avoiding pre-sleep screens prevents the poor sleep quality that triggers frequent night waking. The issue isn't whether to watch TV; it's not watching in that final hour.

12:28 Pre-sleep negotiation directly worsens children's sleep
Allowing "one more book" or "one more water" seems reasonable but quietly pushes bedtime later and drifts into indulgence. Research: higher pre-sleep compliance, worse child sleep—because it signals "I care about your feelings, but I won't set boundaries." That's the definition of indulgent parenting. Persist five days to two weeks; children will trust parents won't budge and stop negotiating.

14:30 Bedroom environment is a sleep stimulus you can control
After three months, kids wake to sudden, repeated noise; use white noise. Keep the room dark, temperature cool rather than warm. Around age two, nightmares and nightlight requests are normal; offer a dim light or closet light, kept very faint. Beyond that, clutter itself harms sleep; organize the room and cut visual stimulation. Make everything sleep-related boring.

20:30 Teenage bedtime rituals need conversation, not commands
With older kids, ask directly: What three things signal that your day is done and you can relax? Options: shower, skincare, combing hair, reading, soft music, brushing teeth, prepping for tomorrow. Keep it consistent nightly as a shutdown signal. Same principles—consistent order, minimal stimulation—extend to teens, but shift from directive to collaborative.

22:37 With teens, use driver's license incentives instead of commands
Telling a 16-year-old "bedtime" rarely works. Pre-agree on required sleep and pre-bed tasks, then tie them to incentives—say, driving to school only if sleep targets and tasks are met. New drivers want driving freedom; it's built-in motivation. The same applies to older children; swap in other "treated as grown-up" freedoms as incentives.

item.title: An infrared company discovers it's only worth 10% of the business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-bizthisway-红外公司转型做质检设备时发现-自己只值10-的生意/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-bizthisway-红外公司转型做质检设备时发现-自己只值10-的生意/
item.description: In full-body infrared medical screening, Gaode Zhigan's (高德质感) technology provides only 10% of the diagnostic service's value, with the other 90% coming from medical expertise and field service—so the company abandoned trying to handle everything and instead shifted to selling only core components.
item.content:encoded:
In full-body infrared medical screening, Gaode Zhigan's (高德质感) technology provides only 10% of the diagnostic service's value, with the other 90% coming from medical expertise and field service—so the company abandoned trying to handle everything and instead shifted to selling only core components.

How a subsidiary of a traditional hard-tech public company spent a decade iterating through civilian use cases with clear decision logic and concrete details—for anyone concerned with commercializing technology.

4:16 Every object emits light you cannot see
The physics of infrared is that any object with temperature emits infrared light due to molecular thermal motion; the longer the wavelength diverges from the visible spectrum, the higher its correlation with temperature. What a detector does is capture the extremely faint infrared signal from an object miles away, causing a temperature change of just fractions of a degree on the detector's surface and reading it out. It must both maintain temperature to preserve the faint signal and dissipate heat quickly to enable continuous imaging—this is the technically hardest part.

6:52 Finding a lost cat was a use case the makers didn't anticipate
Infrared equipment was initially positioned for hunting and finding wildlife, but customers reported that when domestic cats go missing and hide in grass, they can't be found by calling or by eye. A sweep with infrared reveals a bright dot—get there and it's the cat. This civilian use case was not designed by the company; users discovered it themselves and fed back the insight.

14:25 Infrared catches power grid failures before equipment breaks
Electrical anomalies like poor contact or short circuits first produce localized temperature spikes, and infrared inspection discovers aging components before equipment truly breaks down, causing breaker trips and blackouts—allowing engineers to plan replacement of backup equipment and avoid large-scale outages. Huang Sheng (黄胜) noted that the 1970s-80s generation experienced frequent childhood power outages, whereas now there are fewer, which relates to infrared technology's widespread adoption in power systems.

27:44 When you provide 10% of the value, you shouldn't fight for the other 90%
In scenarios like full-body infrared medical screening, infrared is just one critical technical point in the diagnostic process; medical expertise, theoretical backing, and field service constitute ninety percent of the entire diagnostic and customer service chain. The company concluded that rather than filling gaps in capabilities it doesn't understand, it's better to do only what it does best—that ten percent—and sell equipment or chip modules to partners who truly understand medicine and Chinese medicine theory, letting them handle the remaining ninety percent. This decision determines which tracks the company runs end-to-end products (like airport body-temperature screening, where the process is simple and requires no diagnostic judgment) and which it supplies components for.

32:45 Competitors losing money does not mean the market doesn't exist
When the company evaluated potential businesses, it didn't just look at whether it would make or lose money; it also analyzed why competitors lose money—is it because the market itself has no demand, or because others haven't found the right approach? Judging whether you have an advantage to turn a money-losing business into a profitable one is the key step in deciding whether to enter a new scenario, rather than simply abandoning the entire direction because others are losing money.

34:18 Once spun off, nobody sets problems for them to solve anymore
After Gaode Zhigan (高德质感) spun off from Gaode Hongwai (高德红外) as an independent civilian company, the organization initially retained the habit of passively receiving requirements—business units would ask power grids what they needed and directly make that the product direction. But it turned out that different provincial power grids had very different needs, making it impossible to produce a single form factor satisfying all customers, with R&D costs too high. The company therefore established a dedicated product department and marketing department to synthesize scattered front-line requirements into a single product proposal acceptable to most customers, then hand it to R&D—essentially the organization had to learn to set its own problems.

37:23 AI improves how images look, but doesn't command higher prices
AI applications at Gaode Zhigan fall into two categories: one is imperceptible to users, such as using machine learning to optimize image brightness adjustment in high-light and low-light scenarios, making pictures look more comfortable—but this upgrade won't make the product sell for more; it's only a user-experience improvement. The other category is recognizing the photographed object (such as transformers or insulators) and providing more appropriate algorithms and shooting recommendations, helping power-grid engineers complete inspections more efficiently—an auxiliary function rather than an independent selling point.

42:18 Data centers consume electricity, which means infrared has business opportunities
Infrared directly relates to energy flows: major producers like petroleum, natural gas, solar, and wind power, as well as major consumers like metallurgy, all need infrared for monitoring and maintenance. Huang Sheng (黄胜) believes that as AI compute centers become a new major energy consumer and scale up, they will also pull the infrared industry along—though not as directly as how the optical-module industry was directly boosted by AI.

item.title: Partnership law firms can collapse even with zero debt and rising profits
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-oddlots-合伙制律所能在零负债-利润仍增长时突然倒闭/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-oddlots-合伙制律所能在零负债-利润仍增长时突然倒闭/
item.description: A 95-year-old Wall Street law firm with no major debt and rising profits collapsed within months like a bank run because its growth lagged competitors, proving partnerships fail from relative underperformance, not absolute financial decline.
item.content:encoded:
A 95-year-old Wall Street law firm with no major debt and rising profits collapsed within months like a bank run because its growth lagged competitors, proving partnerships fail from relative underperformance, not absolute financial decline.

The guest's academic papers predicted this collapse nearly point-by-point, concentrated on equity structure and bankruptcy mechanics rather than law firm gossip, densely argued and worth hearing in full.

5:04 Partnership law firms persist for historical and regulatory reasons, not efficiency
Partnership structures everywhere require partner ownership for three reasons. First, historically, starting a law practice required only labor, not capital. Second, state bar ethics rules mandate that lawyers own their firms. But the deeper explanation comes from Yale economist Henry Hansman: lawyers' output (billable hours traced to specific clients) is measurable in ways factory workers' output isn't, so partnerships create fewer internal profit-allocation disputes than worker ownership models. This measurability advantage is why Hansman's theory predicts partnerships over employee ownership schemes like at General Motors.

12:14 A key partner's departure triggers the run because costs don't fall with revenue
When a star partner leaves, clients follow almost immediately—revenue vanishes overnight. But office leases, pension obligations, and the salaries of junior partners who depended on that partner's client base don't shrink. If that partner was generating more revenue than his own compensation, his departure is pure loss. The profit pool that remaining partners split shrinks directly, forcing compensation cuts—and that's where the run begins.

14:17 Partner distributions become clawable at bankruptcy once the firm goes insolvent
Partners don't receive wages; they receive discretionary profit distributions, legally equivalent to dividends. Once a firm is declared insolvent, any further distributions to partners can be clawed back by creditors under fraudulent transfer law. This creates a calculation every partner silently runs: money in my pocket now might have to go back later.

18:23 Each partner constantly weighs leaving by expected value of compensation
Take a partner at Weil in September expecting $2 million in January. But if the firm has a 50% chance of collapsing by February, that $2 million is really worth only $1 million in expectation. If Gibson Dunn offers $1.5 million with lower failure risk, that's actually higher expected value—appearing to be a pay cut while genuinely being a raise. Every partner is quietly solving this problem. Once enough partners get the same answer, the run begins.

21:25 Falling in the rankings is more fatal than falling profits
Economist Morley's papers predicted exactly this scenario: a firm could collapse despite zero major debt and continued profit growth, provided growth lagged competitors. Weil's per-partner profit ranking fell from #9 in 2020 to #20 in 2025, while profits kept rising every year—just not as fast as Kirkland's. Weil got stuck: too small to be a megaplatform, too big to be a boutique like Wachtell or Cravath.

28:31 Partners' equity vanishes at retirement, so nobody invests for the future
A Microsoft shareholder can hold forever; future value gets priced into trading. A law firm partner's equity expires at retirement—no buyback, no perpetuity. This creates generational conflict: a 31-year-old partner might invest in the firm's future; a 61-year-old retiring in two years has zero incentive. This explains why law firms won't spend heavily to build AI systems that pay off in five years—because today's decision-makers won't be there to enjoy the returns.

36:42 Investor-owned law firms survive runs because partners aren't owners
Australian law firm Slater & Gordon is listed and investor-owned. Its Quindel acquisition turned out to be fraud, leaving the company insolvent. But because lawyers don't own the firm, management could wipe out shareholder equity and hand creditors the company as new shareholders in a restructuring—while lawyers kept their salaries and jobs, like Delta Airlines pilots. At a partnership like Weil, if you tried the same move, every partner walks to Cravath the next morning.

47:54 Law firms will lease AI like office space, not build it
Generational conflict means today's partners won't fund AI that pays off in five years, since different partners will be there then. Firms will license and rent AI technology like they lease offices—not own it like they'd buy a building. Kirkland & Ellis' $500 million AI program over five years looks ambitious until you note their ~$10 billion annual revenue—it's a rounding error, and they've paced it to sync with revenue growth, not to get ahead of it.

item.title: Huang's Ouster Isn't Scandal but Washington's Long-Overdue Reckoning with Nvidia
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-sharptech-黄仁勋下台不是桃色事件-是华盛顿对英伟达积怨已久的总清算/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-sharptech-黄仁勋下台不是桃色事件-是华盛顿对英伟达积怨已久的总清算/
item.description: Nvidia's repeated defiance of China export policy and the national security system was the true trigger for Huang's forced exit; the sex scandal was merely the final straw.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia's repeated defiance of China export policy and the national security system was the true trigger for Huang's forced exit; the sex scandal was merely the final straw.

The first half systematically traces Nvidia's origins and governance structure; the middle section's debate over chip export-control logic is the most valuable part of the episode—listen through to get the full picture.

4:11 An affair with subordinates is ironclad grounds for board removal
The hosts first clarify an often-overlooked governance issue: boards are supposed to represent shareholders, but they also have motives that don't align with shareholder interests—like protecting their own seats. But this time is different. In US corporate culture, romantic relationships with subordinates cross a clear, irrefutable red line. Once established, a board has almost no choice but to fire, even if the stock price drops double digits, even if employees and most shareholders would prefer otherwise.

16:31 Nvidia doesn't sell chips, it sells systems
Around 2019, Huang's crucial move was acquiring Mellanox: he recognized not faster individual chips, but the system capability of linking multiple chips via high-speed interconnect into a single logical system, later evolving into MVLink. Nvidia's moat isn't just CUDA but this: selling systems, not chips. AMD's previous-generation chips had better single-chip performance, but AMD doesn't build systems—that game AMD simply never entered.

20:35 Huang went all-out to keep Nvidia from becoming another Intel
If buyers were only Amazon, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic—a handful of megacustomers—they'd have the negotiating power to crush Nvidia's margins, exactly what happened to Intel when negotiating with AMD. Huang aggressively backed Neoclouds and various new labs, deliberately creating more buyers to avoid becoming a small number of giants' captive supplier. This wasn't charity.

1:03:01 Downgraded-spec chips destroyed Nvidia's relationship with national security officials
Biden's first version of China chip sanctions limited memory bandwidth, not compute. Within a month, Huang released lower-bandwidth, worse-performing ‘compliant’ chips and continued selling heavily into China. Technically legal, but the security establishment saw this as open defiance. From that day on, the national security system branded Nvidia a ‘bad actor’ and Huang branded them ‘idiots.’ Their relationship became adversarial—this was the beginning of what became the final reckoning.

1:09:01 Export bans have made Chinese chip independence a necessity
The core argument against chip bans: you can't conjure a chip ecosystem just by throwing money at it—Microsoft spent billions and couldn't save Windows Phone. As long as Nvidia chips are available, no Chinese government mandate can force programmers to abandon CUDA for alternatives. But a complete cutoff creates a hard necessity for independence—undoing fifty years of US tech-transfer management strategy.

1:17:05 Corruption allegations changed the character of the entire affair
Beyond chip exports and policy shifts, a third layer of anger stems from more direct corruption suspicions—like the Trump family's financial interests in Malaysian data centers. The hosts argue that even if you can understand the Trump team's positions on China policy, adding corruption poisons the entire affair. Huang's scandal became a single outlet for all the accumulated resentment.

1:18:05 Nvidia's supplier financing model faces its biggest test
Nvidia has played banker to its ecosystem, rolling free cash flow into debt into equity investments, essentially bridging the entire AI bubble. Whether the interim CEO and CFO will continue Huang's aggressive supplier financing is an open question—and credit tightening in the Neocloud market actually began three months before the scandal, making the stock drop less damaging than what's coming.

item.title: Physical AI founder bets hardware first: when foundation models arrive, pure models thin
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-latetalk-物理ai创始人提前押注硬件-基模一来-模型就会变薄/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-latetalk-物理ai创始人提前押注硬件-基模一来-模型就会变薄/
item.description: When Liu Songming founded LiberAI, he predicted foundation models like GPT-6 Astra would consume System 2—the perception and planning layer of embodied AI. From day one, he chose hardware and product as the moat instead of building a pure model company.
item.content:encoded:
When Liu Songming founded LiberAI, he predicted foundation models like GPT-6 Astra would consume System 2—the perception and planning layer of embodied AI. From day one, he chose hardware and product as the moat instead of building a pure model company.

Information density concentrates in the second half: how glove data approximates or surpasses teleoperation at lower cost, and why hardware-model coupling runs deeper than the founder expected. The first 25 minutes on growth history can be skipped.

25:17 Technical judgment, not industry connections, drives early-stage capital decisions
Industry convention pairs young technical talent with a veteran industry executive. Liu chose differently. At this stage, the company's biggest expenditure is compute and data collection. Deciding where that money goes and which technical paths to pursue requires technical judgment, not just resource coordination. Without it, capital efficiency collapses.

35:23 Foundation models will consume the perception layer, squeezing pure robotics companies
Liu maps robot-world interaction into three layers: System 2 (perception, planning, reasoning), System 1 (converting instructions to action sequences), System 0 (low-level motor control). Through 2023-24, venture capital believed embodied companies could own all three layers and scale toward AGI. Liu predicted from day one that foundation models would inevitably capture System 2. GPT-6 Astra's arrival proved it. This makes pure-model robotics startups dangerously thin. LiberAI chose full-stack from inception—using hardware and product to thicken the narrowing moat.

59:37 Glove data with 25% teleoperation outperforms 100% teleoperation alone
Experiments show glove data combined with 25% real-robot teleoperation data outperforms models trained on 100% real-robot teleoperation alone. Teleoperation isn't perfect: operators watch sideways while robots move forward, creating a viewpoint mismatch with the robot's camera. Lack of force feedback makes operators slow. This motion pattern diverges from smooth human actions in internet videos. Gloves worn on human hands align naturally with human motion and extract knowledge from internet videos more effectively.

1:19:43 Hardware constraints go deeper into performance than training recipes can fix
The biggest surprise wasn't training—it was hardware. Different morphologies and sensor choices affect final performance far more than expected, and this impact can't be recovered through later training approaches. System 0 motor control algorithms couple deeply with System 1 action generation. Motor control couples tightly with the robot's joint structure, DOF, and motor parameters. This demonstrates hardware companies' structural advantage over pure model companies—but it also means iteration speed is constrained by hardware's long development cycles.

1:36:56 Foundation model labs lack the character for robotics' unglamorous delivery work
Consider rumors of OpenAI or Anthropic acquiring Physical Intelligence, and potential entry by carmakers or Huawei. Liu argues that real competition only emerges at delivery scale, where every customer is a hardened negotiation. This work demands patience that OpenAI likely lacks, and the incentives don't align: the same engineering effort applied to software yields 20x growth. Why chase service and manufacturing margins? Liu judges the real threat is non-standard automation specialists and prior-generation delivery firms.

1:48:01 Physical robotics will eventually consolidate into an Apple-scale giant
Liu expects physical AI applications to transition from today's fragmented commercial and industrial niches toward consolidation. Eventually a mega-company emerges at Apple's scale—among the greatest industrial products in human history. This company likely emerges from firms already pursuing full-stack, hardware-first approaches. This is what LiberAI positions as its highest-probability wager.

2:00:06 Build organizations that question decisions made too fast with too little information
Liu reflects on past errors: mistakes often stem not from bad option selection but from deciding too fast on incomplete information. People unconsciously filter incoming data through existing expectations. This trap is especially dangerous in familiar domains, where strong priors tempt you to skip verification. The remedy: deliberately preserve diverse voices and cultivate people who can stand up and audit—to coordinate information gaps and misaligned goals—rather than relying on one founder's final call.

item.title: Liangpei wants users to leave fast—that's exactly how it makes money
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-wangqinwen-良配巴不得用户尽快离开-这恰恰是它的赚钱逻辑/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-wangqinwen-良配巴不得用户尽快离开-这恰恰是它的赚钱逻辑/
item.description: Liangpei (良配) sells memberships that can't be renewed; users leave once they match. The faster they go, the fewer tokens the platform burns—exactly opposite to most AI products profiting from retention.
item.content:encoded:
Liangpei (良配) sells memberships that can't be renewed; users leave once they match. The faster they go, the fewer tokens the platform burns—exactly opposite to most AI products profiting from retention.

A story of a former Kimi employee who spent 8 years accumulating resources and raised 15 million in 3 hours; the middle section clarifies traditional matchmaker schemes, and the second half breaks down AI dating business models in detail, with information density concentrated in the middle and later sections.

3:00 Traditional matchmakers price by what you can pay, not what service costs
Zeng Xinxun notes that among 150 couples who registered at Shenzhen's Civil Affairs Bureau, fewer than 5 percent succeeded through professional matchmakers. Traditional matchmakers don't price based on the service itself, but first probe your willingness to pay and credit card limits—the same service sells for 20,000, 30,000 or 50,000 yuan depending on how much you can afford. More egregiously, some agencies pressure young women to take loans, using the pitch ‘it's better to find a husband than buy a handbag’ to package dating as an investment.

21:15 Grassroots teams lack resources to compete with well-funded rivals
Zeng ran a campus food delivery platform in university that generated over 10 million yuan in annual revenue at peak, but was completely shut out when Ele.me raised 80 million dollars and rapidly expanded to 200 cities. He concluded this wasn't a product or execution problem, but that grassroots teams lack the resources to race against opponents already backed by capital markets—which is why he spent 8 years before this venture deliberately ‘accumulating equipment’ (technology, team, industry credentials).

37:23 Three hours to raise 15 million required eight years of prep
A week after resigning as CTO of Kimi, Zeng met with investors; by chance at a hackathon café, he talked for 15 minutes with someone from Jujin Capital, who immediately called to verify his Kimi background and set up a meeting with Xu Xin the next day. In three hours of negotiation, Xu Xin proactively offered to provide the full 15 million yuan representing 20 percent equity in one payment, with zero protective clauses in the agreement. Zeng says this wasn't luck, but the accumulated technology, team, and industry credentials he'd built over 8 years all materializing at that moment.

44:29 Four structural flaws prevent dating apps from helping you pair up
Zeng identifies four categories of problems in existing dating products: platforms mix users with different needs to boost DAU, with profiles limited to 100-150 characters creating severe information shortage; an endless stream of candidates creates the illusion of abundance, making people constantly compare and undervalue the person in front of them; and the platform's business model rewards longer user stays, giving it no incentive to actually help you find someone, putting user and platform interests fundamentally at odds.

47:31 Single-match design escapes the user-platform prisoner's dilemma
Liangpei designed the EV1 matching mechanism, which doesn't offer a continuous candidate pool but shows one person at a time. Zeng believes previous products didn't dare try this because match success rates were too low—EV1's risk directly exposes you to the 1-minus-success-rate failure probability; Liangpei only dared build EV1 because AI collected two to three thousand characters of context, raising match accuracy high enough to support it.

50:36 Only non-renewable memberships make platforms want you to succeed
Liangpei's core memberships are non-renewable: the 2,000 yuan ‘guaranteed marriage membership’ keeps the payment if users marry within three years, otherwise fully refunded; there's also a 1,000 yuan perpetual membership paid in one lump sum. Zeng explains the design works because the platform burns tokens daily for each user, and the longer users stay the higher the cost, so the platform naturally wants users matched quickly and gone—the opposite of most software that profits from renewal and time spent.

53:37 Acquisition cost rose from a few yuan to over 50
In 2018-19 doing campus delivery, acquiring a user cost just a few yuan, but today in the two-sided market Liangpei faces, 50 yuan acquisition cost isn't enough. In the first week after launch, Zeng watched growth curves daily with anxiety, because the earliest users trusted the product most but experienced the smallest sample size and matching pool, until a few articles went viral and user scale picked up.

56:39 Betting everything on one path beats hedging between many options
Zeng says at every major inflection point in his life he chose only one path—applied to only Southern University of Science and Technology for college, picked one place when job hunting and went there, and for this venture only does dating, something he experienced personally, rather than the billion-dollar-market spaces investors suggested. He believes that with multiple choices you fall into decision paralysis, efficiency drops lowest, and going all-in actually provides clarity.

item.title: Riding a trend is 1% of success; being the right person is 99%
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-zhangxiaojun-踩中风口在成功里只占1-99-是你是不是那块料/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-13-zhangxiaojun-踩中风口在成功里只占1-99-是你是不是那块料/
item.description: Liang Qiwei draws on years of game-making to argue: trends and capital narratives can sustain short-term revenue, but what truly determines fate is the creator's character, not external circumstances.
item.content:encoded:
Liang Qiwei draws on years of game-making to argue: trends and capital narratives can sustain short-term revenue, but what truly determines fate is the creator's character, not external circumstances.

Most of the conversation explores wuxia aesthetics and literary theory; the truly valuable startup retrospective and self-examination come in the second half—listen past the midpoint.

1:05 The core of the knight-errant is not goodness, but willingness to risk greatly
Liang Qiwei rejects equating the knight-errant with the everyday good person (like helping an elderly woman cross the street). True knights-errant must, driven by hatred and injustice, choose to bear risk with superhuman resolve—if you're not exposed to real danger, you're just a good person. This also explains why knights-errant are always outsiders: the rivers and lakes stand against the state; knights have no power to enforce law, only to maintain justice where order collapses.

33:31 Players see through any moral label you attach
When the team tried to add direct dialogue like "For nation and people, that is the great knight-errant" to give the game moral weight, players almost universally rejected it. The problem wasn't disagreement with the sentiment itself, Liang explains, but that players saw through the creative intent: you're not thinking about the game itself, you're trying to borrow external moral associations for mainstream approval. The lesson became: convey the spirit obliquely, never through self-congratulatory statements.

1:12:10 In school he was the invisible man in the dorm
Liang Qiwei recalls having Asperger's-like traits—indifferent to the real world, acutely sensitive to the virtual. In his dorm, he wasn't bullied; he was "transparent." Roommates gradually stopped inviting him to meals, and he felt no loneliness, because loneliness presumes a desire for companionship he simply didn't experience. The term itself mischaracterized his state.

1:52:48 One failed exam erased his entire life plan
Liang was on track: fifth in his class, accepted to Tsinghua for graduate study through the direct enrollment track. Then he failed engineering economics, an unprecedented system failure—the rules said you could advance to Tsinghua but couldn't graduate. Like learning there is no final boss before the climax, the world suddenly unraveled. But it was also the first time fate loosened its grip on his predetermined path as a "problem-solver."

2:34:31 During the capital boom, the team forgot how to do real work
After Blade of Shadow I found early success—twenty people, a couple million yuan monthly profit—the company dreamed bigger: anime, series, IP matrices, even pitching for a New Third Board listing. For years, Liang's actual work was pitching to investors, cutting deals at dinners, spinning IP narratives. Real coding and art happened less than a day per week. He compares it to martial artists who haven't drawn a real blade in years; when actual combat comes, they're finished in one stroke.

2:44:38 Professing purity is the start of impurity
Liang reflects on an article he wrote years ago: humble-bragging about colleagues' raises and a new girlfriend abroad. He sees it now as commodifying pure creative experience into capital-market small talk—using claims of "purity" to prove he'd learned the money game. Two selves were fighting: one faithful to first principles, one increasingly shrewd, hunting for external validation.

3:01:53 Chasing trends is 1% of success; capability is 99%
Blade of Shadow II deliberately stacked two trends: mobile esports and anime culture. It succeeded at neither. Liang's conclusion: catching a trend accounts for maybe 1% of success; 99% depends on internal capability—whether the team actually has what it takes to execute the vision. External conditions are irrelevant if you're not the person built for this work. No market opens for those not suited to seize it.

3:23:06 Brilliant Murong Fu always loses to clumsy Guo Jing
Game Science and miHoYo succeeded through what Liang calls "strong-mind thinking": the conviction that markets aren't fixed, that force of will can reshape them. Liang admits to the opposite—the "problem-solver" mentality: solve what's given, never imagine changing the game itself. In wuxia metaphor, Murong Fu—brilliant, elaborate, overthinking—always falls to apparently simple Guo Jing. True strength is internal, inward-facing, not in displayed talent.

item.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO over espionage scandal; company has no successor internally
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-hardfork-黄仁勋因间谍绯闻辞任英伟达ceo-公司内部找不到能接替他的人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-hardfork-黄仁勋因间谍绯闻辞任英伟达ceo-公司内部找不到能接替他的人/
item.description: The incoming CFO can only be an interim CEO, because Nvidia's helmsman must be both a top computer scientist and a strong enough executive to browbeat Taiwan suppliers—a combination only Jensen Huang possesses today.
item.content:encoded:
The incoming CFO can only be an interim CEO, because Nvidia's helmsman must be both a top computer scientist and a strong enough executive to browbeat Taiwan suppliers—a combination only Jensen Huang possesses today.

One episode gives you the complete chain of events, the board's motives, and the succession puzzle—high information density, though the ending's jokes about memes can be skipped.

1:00 Resignation wasn't one scandal—it was scandal stacked upon scandal
The trigger for Huang's resignation wasn't a single scandal but escalation in layers: first the revelation of a relationship with Alice Wong (suspected Chinese spy), then a separate exposure of a long-running affair with Kimberly Powell, the medical-division VP reporting directly to him. The board convened overnight and announced his resignation before market open. The show frames this as a twist in a spy story—two relationships stacked together finally broke his position.

6:19 The board wanted to keep him, but finances changed the math
Multiple board members hold over $1 billion in Nvidia stock each. Huang has been the only CEO in the company's 33-year history, so by normal logic they would have moved to protect him. But the scandal had already tanked the stock price, and keeping him would only expand the losses. Stephen Witt argues the board's decision was a financial calculation to protect shareholder value, not a moral judgment.

8:31 The commerce secretary ran interference for Huang inside government
Commerce Secretary Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Bessent clashed directly over whether to add Megaspeed to the trade blacklist and whether to close regulatory loopholes in Southeast Asia data centers. Lutnick had been seen as the force inside government delaying export controls to protect Huang's interests. With Huang's fall, Congressional and internal-government pressure to tighten China-related chip restrictions has visibly intensified.

17:02 He saw the world as he wished it to be
Anna Swanson argues Huang consistently denied the existence of chip-smuggling problems for years, even as US authorities uncovered large-scale smuggling cases. Her assessment: this trait—seeing the world as one wishes it to be—was both the source of his long success and possibly the root of his collapse.

26:24 Finding a successor is like replacing Michael Jordan
Stephen Witt frames the succession problem this way: it's like asking ‘who replaces Michael Jordan after he leaves the Bulls?’—there's no ready replacement. Huang had to be a top computer scientist, a fierce enough executive to browbeat Taiwan suppliers, someone able to schmooze clients and call Trump directly. These skills rarely appear in one person; the company essentially needs three people to fill his void.

28:35 The CFO doesn't understand transistors; she can only be temporary
Interim CEO Colette Kress is widely seen as a transitional choice: she's an excellent financial executive but not a world-class computer scientist, and a chip company's CEO must truly understand the technical details from transistors to data centers. Inside Nvidia, talents like Ian Buck excel at engineering but lack experience with customers and suppliers. Finding someone with both sets of skills is extremely difficult.

31:53 Financial disclosures shifted quietly as the scandal simmered
As the scandal festered last year, Nvidia abruptly changed how it disclosed revenue—making it harder to track what percentage of revenue came from Singapore and Malaysia. Anna Swanson points out this is precisely when the Southeast Asian business surge into China (that journalists were trying to document) got deliberately obscured. Colette Kress, as CFO, would have been deeply involved in such financial-disclosure decisions.

38:06 Thirty days ago he wielded enormous power; today he has none
Stephen Witt describes the collapse as Greek tragedy: thirty days ago Huang was one of the most powerful people in AI; now he holds 3% of Nvidia—still valuable—but has no executive power and Trump won't take his calls anymore. The show suggests this illustrates a deeper truth: even in the age of AI, the endings are written by human weakness, not technology itself.
