item.content:encoded:
Suharto pushed a million-hectare rice project to sustain his 'Father of Development' reputation, but peatlands proved unsuitable for farming and planning failures triggered what became one of Southeast Asia's largest single-year carbon-release fire events.

A real case of political obsession overriding scientific judgment, with staggering numbers and straightforward narrative—easy to follow in one commute.

4:12 Rice shortages destabilized Sukarno and enabled Suharto to seize power
Under Sukarno, rice was more than food—it was hard currency for military and bureaucratic salaries and was prioritized for foreign exchange. Sukarno's rice quotas mobilized the country but backfired: rice did not reach deficit regions, foreign exchange went to imported rice instead of needed fertilizer, Javanese paddies degraded, and output fell 13.6% between 1960 and 1964. The crisis destabilized his regime and handed Suharto the opening for his coup.

6:18 Oil windfall from 1973 embargo made Indonesia's rice self-sufficiency possible
Suharto took power just as the Green Revolution introduced high-yield varieties IR8 and IR5, and Indonesia caught the 1973 Middle East oil embargo windfall: annual petroleum revenue spiked above $5 billion. This money subsidized fertilizer permanently, set a rice price floor, and built irrigation canals and roads. Rice output soared from 12 million tons in 1969 to 22 million tons by 1981. By 1984, Indonesia declared rice self-sufficiency—the foundation of Suharto's "Father of Development" reputation.

7:22 Rice production stalled in the 1990s while population kept growing
By the 1990s, rice output growth collapsed to 0.5–1% annually while population grew 1–2% yearly. Late-1980s urban development claimed about 20% of Java's best farmland. Severe floods and droughts compounded the problem. By 1992, Indonesia returned to rice imports for the first time in a decade; the 1995 drought forced imports of 3 million tons. The loss threatened Suharto's political foundation.

13:38 Peatlands unsuitable for rice farming was established science by the 1970s
The Dayak indigenous people had for generations grown rice only on coastal, shallower, relatively fertile peatlands, and even there harvests were often poor due to unpredictable rainfall. Indonesia's Bogor Soil Research Institute had classified such interior peatlands as "problem soils" since 1974. Yet after visiting a successful Singaporean-Chinese operation on Sumatra's coast, Suharto decided to replicate the model on the completely different deep inland peatlands of Central Kalimantan, ignoring the geological difference and existing scientific conclusions.

16:40 Suharto demanded results by 1997 so construction began before studies finished
Suharto demanded the first harvest by 1997, so construction started in January 1996 before cost-benefit analysis, engineering studies, or environmental impact assessments were complete. Most Indonesian companies and international investors refused to participate; a longtime Suharto contractor reportedly joined only to avoid losing other government contracts. Environmental group WALI tried exposing the threat to endangered orangutans and ecosystems, but could not stop the project.

17:41 Massive drainage canals destroyed peatlands while resettlement housing barely got built
Thousands of kilometers of drainage canals were poorly planned—they cut directly across major peatland domes and systematically drained the layers of water. The plan called for 20,000 homes for Javanese settlers within two years; after ten months, only 600 were built. For Suharto's April 1997 inspection, authorities built a helicopter pad and temporarily replanted rice seedlings to show prosperity. He stayed two hours, announced the project a success, and left.

18:41 Half a million hectares burned in 1997, sending smoke across Southeast Asia
Forest cleared, peatlands dried, illegal burning for clearance sparked fires that satellites detected as early as January 1997. In 1997 alone, over 500,000 hectares of the 1.4 million-hectare zone burned, 80% of it peatland. The carbon released from peat averaging 51 centimeters thick was enormous. Fires flared repeatedly until the June 1998 rains; the total burned area reached roughly 10 million hectares, smoke drifted to Singapore and Malaysia, and the region's carbon emissions were among the largest single-year increases on record.

21:51 Billions spent but left Dayak people and settlers both empty-handed
The project was budgeted at $2–3 billion, partly from Indonesia's "Reforestation Fund." Much money vanished into corruption and fake subcontracts. The Dayak were promised investment and prosperity; instead their farmland burned, fishponds were destroyed by canals, and traditional territory fell to settlers. Some 15,000 Javanese families who relocated found almost no infrastructure. After Suharto fell in 1998 amid the Asian financial crisis, the new government formally canceled the project in 1999.

item.title: Anthropic is using AI to build AI, doubling its research speed
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-eightythousand-metr-发现-anthropic-用-ai-造-ai-速度已翻倍/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-eightythousand-metr-发现-anthropic-用-ai-造-ai-速度已翻倍/
item.description: METR's investigation finds that roughly 80% of Anthropic's current research acceleration comes from using its own AI to conduct research, which is precisely the early sign of recursive self-improvement that observers have warned about for years.
item.content:encoded:
METR's investigation finds that roughly 80% of Anthropic's current research acceleration comes from using its own AI to conduct research, which is precisely the early sign of recursive self-improvement that observers have warned about for years.

An independent institution spent 11 weeks examining Anthropic's internal data to produce this report; its core conclusions and supporting evidence include concrete numbers that could change how you assess AI risk, making it worth hearing in full.

0:00 Anthropic's research speed has doubled year-on-year
After 11 weeks examining Anthropic's internal test scores, training data, and employee interviews, METR concluded that as of October, Anthropic's speed on quantifiable tasks had roughly doubled from a year prior, with a confidence interval of 1.3 to 3x. One piece of evidence: plotting all of the company's model test scores (including three unpublished internal models) on a timeline, the slope suddenly doubled from October last year. METR also ruled out increased compute as the main driver—while compute has indeed increased, it cannot explain this acceleration.

2:57 Two years' progress compressed: what doubling really means
By late 2023, Claude was just a chatbot that couldn't read images or browse the web; by late 2025, it could work independently for over 30 hours and build a complete Slack-like application without human intervention. That's two years of progress. Then just one year later, AI helped solve a math problem that had puzzled mathematicians for 87 years. This is what METR means by walking through two years of progress in one year.

4:00 80% of the acceleration comes from AI assisting its own research
After ruling out simple explanations like increased compute, hiring surges, new data, and research breakthroughs, METR's best guess is that roughly 80% of the current acceleration comes from Anthropic using its own AI to assist research. But in the public report, most of the reasoning around this figure and the most persuasive evidence have been redacted by Anthropic; METR admits this forces outsiders to rely more on their judgment.

4:48 Researcher testimony aligns with end-to-end automation metrics
Internal Anthropic researchers said that in certain areas AI has dramatically accelerated work; one researcher's exact words are quoted. While this type of anecdotal evidence alone isn't compelling, it aligns with the timeline: the acceleration appears to have begun in October 2025, precisely when Claude could write code continuously and independently for hours. Anthropic's own data shows that earlier this year, Claude barely conducted research end-to-end, but by August could complete roughly a quarter of it under human supervision.

6:19 No clear factor will break this cycle in the near term
AI building AI differs from other technologies: the stronger the AI, the faster it can help you build the next generation. This cycle only gets stuck at three bottlenecks—compute, training data, or algorithmic insights. METR examined all three and found no signs of constraint within the next year; they admit to low confidence and changing views with new information, but cannot rule out further acceleration in the next six months, or even acceleration of the acceleration itself.

7:33 Toby Ord's challenge and METR's response
Philosopher Toby Ord pointed out that the test score line might have another explanation: Mythos comes from a much larger training run, and large training runs typically deliver a one-time capability jump. Excluding that factor, the acceleration is only 1.4x rather than 2x. But AI safety researcher Buck Shlegeris responded that test scores were never METR's main basis for their conclusion—they're only the part of the report that wasn't redacted and that the public could see. The evidence that made METR more confident in doubling was what got deleted.

10:41 Anthropic admits it has crossed its own safety threshold
Anthropic drew its own line: AI accelerating research to walk through two years of progress in one year. Its August public report claimed the acceleration was "below 2x," but using Anthropic's private data, METR calculated 1.97x. Just before the author finished this episode, Anthropic admitted in its latest IPO filing that based on expectations for the next generation of models and current velocity, the company has already crossed the line it drew for itself—but only said it is evaluating the impact, not what it will do.

11:45 Companies won't constrain themselves; regulation must step in
The logic for why AI companies won't stop is clear: if we stop, competitors will continue, and they might be even less careful. New York State legislator Alex Bores called for Congress to pass legislation banning AI companies from fully automating their own research; this proposal has supporters from Bernie Sanders to Steve Bannon. METR also points out that whether they get invited into the company, what they can see, and what the report says are all decided by Anthropic—the company even tightened its redaction rules in the final week, forcing METR to redo work and delay publication.

item.title: Data centers became one of the biggest losers in America's midterm elections
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-sciencevs-数据中心成了美国中期选举最大输家之一/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-sciencevs-数据中心成了美国中期选举最大输家之一/
item.description: Congress's approval power hasn't changed, but the execution layer has been infiltrated by political screening; even with Democrats controlling both chambers, they cannot shake Trump's actual control over science—voters ultimately decided based on electricity costs and noise from AI data centers.
item.content:encoded:
Congress's approval power hasn't changed, but the execution layer has been infiltrated by political screening; even with Democrats controlling both chambers, they cannot shake Trump's actual control over science—voters ultimately decided based on electricity costs and noise from AI data centers.

No explosive reversals, but it explains the specific mechanism of "funds uncut but unreachable" and the details of how data centers unexpectedly became an election issue—worth listening to.

4:12 Funding totals unchanged, but money's destination has shifted
One-and-a-half years ago, NIH already terminated over a thousand projects related to climate change, vaccine uptake, and health issues. American aid cuts are predicted to cause 25 million deaths over the next fifteen years. Now it's becoming more opaque: these cuts have been institutionalized as routine screening procedures.

5:17 Scientific approval isn't the final gate; politics comes next
Even after expert panels score a project as "scientific excellence," the funds must pass through political review by NIH leadership and even RFK Jr.'s office before release, ensuring alignment with government priorities. This screening targets keywords; research touching women's health, LGBTQ rights, or vaccines gets held up—timing that coincides with the recent spike in measles cases.

8:30 Officials claim no cuts, but entire research fields have disappeared
NIH and NSF distribute similar total amounts as before, letting administrators say "no cuts." But fields explicitly required by Congress to receive funding—like women's health and health disparities research—have had their money redirected elsewhere, making some research topics nearly impossible to pursue.

11:35 RFK Jr. remains one of the more popular cabinet members
Democratic candidate Annie Andrews publicly called RFK Jr. a "liar and conspiracy theorist" and pushed for impeachment. But Max notes that despite scientists' disdain, RFK Jr. is actually fairly popular among cabinet members, and he had ambitions to run for president in 2028—meaning he may not leave easily or be forced out.

12:35 Candidates weaponized MAHA's language against MAHA itself
Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed didn't attack RFK Jr.'s MAHA movement head-on. Instead he launched his own Baha campaign—Building a Healthier America—borrowing MAHA-style language about "removing toxins from food" but directing "toxins" specifically at pesticides with scientific evidence behind them, reframing the rhetoric through a scientific lens.

16:50 Majorities named AI data centers a key reason to vote
NBC exit polls found 56% of voters thought AI and data centers were a major or decisive factor in how they voted. Of over 40 ballot measures restricting data center construction, nearly all passed—interpreted as anger over rising electricity costs, noise, and water use, not necessarily opposition to AI itself.

17:55 Data centers have become symbols of giants crushing ordinary people
Many towns report having almost no say in data center decisions, with the process opaque and feeling like big tech crushing small people once again. Silicon Valley and Big Tech bet heavily on Republicans and Trump; as data center controversy builds, public distrust of their motives rises noticeably, especially in Texas where Elon Musk poured in large sums.

21:00 Democrats control Congress but cannot override vetoes or Senate rules
Even with Democrats controlling both chambers, Trump can veto bills, and Democrats lack the two-thirds majority in both houses to override. Non-budget bills must also clear the Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold; budget bills require Trump's signature. This means even if Democrats wanted to double NSF funding, it would likely fail on Trump's desk.

item.title: AI shrinks development cycles, reviving genres studios abandoned
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-a16z-ai-让做游戏从十年压到两年-烂genre要迎来文艺复兴/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-a16z-ai-让做游戏从十年压到两年-烂genre要迎来文艺复兴/
item.description: GTA6 took twelve years. Two a16z partners argue AI can now compress game prototyping to weeks, letting studios fund niche genres and new IPs rather than sequels.
item.content:encoded:
GTA6 took twelve years. Two a16z partners argue AI can now compress game prototyping to weeks, letting studios fund niche genres and new IPs rather than sequels.

Two partners share firsthand experience making games with their kids to explain how AI is reshaping game development. The episode is not information-dense throughout, but includes concrete examples worth your time.

2:04 Direct engine control, not just instructions, is what changed game development
Jonathan Lai identifies a breakthrough from roughly a month ago: models can now directly manipulate Blender, Unreal, and Unity instead of just telling users what to do. This means someone with no game dev experience can use Astra to write a game design doc, generate concept art, model, rig, import to engine, add sound, and export a playable game. Astra can even screenshot itself for QA, spotting and fixing its own bugs. This accounts for why early prototypes on X were so surprisingly polished.

3:05 Long cycles explain why studios won't risk new IP or unfamiliar genres
Jonathan explains that if a AAA game costs a decade and hundreds of millions of dollars to produce, producers become extremely conservative—approving sequels over new IPs, proven genres like first-person shooters over experimental types. Call of Duty is up to around 20 entries. When AI cuts both timelines and budgets, studios will fund unproven teams and new IPs. This unlocks structural innovation in gaming, not just cost savings.

9:12 AI drops the barrier to game-making from professional teams to single creators
Jonathan contends that games are uniquely complex multidisciplinary products, requiring simultaneous expertise in coding, art, design, and audio—a far higher barrier than photography or video. AI fills the skill gaps a solo creator lacks, letting someone with just an idea and reference images iterate toward a prototype. He expects many will quit halfway through, but some will fall in love with game development, causing a surge in creator numbers in the industry.

18:31 Counter-Strike and League of Legends grew from mods, not original designs
Jonathan points to Counter-Strike as a Half-Life mod, League of Legends inspired by Dota (itself a Warcraft III mod), and Fortnite and PUBG both descended from Arma's battle royale mod—all became billion-dollar franchises. AI now lets any fan of an IP simply tell Astra: ‘make me a Ghost of Tsushima with a voxel building system.’ If it's fun, it could grow into a new genre the way those historical mods did.

22:44 Falling development costs will revive expensive, niche genres like RTS
Anish points to genres like RTS, traditionally expensive to produce with poor returns—no one has made a good iPad RTS despite everyone wanting one—now facing possible full revival as dev costs drop. He also mentions ‘profession simulators,’ an extremely niche category he loves. He recently played a Tokyo subway conductor simulator; these games were economically unfeasible before, but with costs now low, even a tiny player base like his can support profitability.

27:47 IP creators historically don't profit from mods made from their own work
Jonathan flags a structural problem: historically, IP creators rarely profit from mods of their own work—Dota's original developers made little from League of Legends, and Half-Life's developers probably didn't make much from Counter-Strike. Now if companies embrace AI-driven remixes, mods, and decompilation-recompilation, the business model is still unclear. Only Minecraft is an exception, having natively benefited from mod ecosystems.

35:50 The real opportunity is new mechanics, not faster versions of existing games
Jonathan frames current studio use of AI for concept art, design docs, and prototypes as the ‘first wave’ of adoption—now standard practice. He argues that the truly exciting ‘second wave’ is using AI to create entirely new game mechanics and genres that don't exist today, expanding the total gaming market rather than just making GTA6 faster and cheaper.

36:51 The ultimate MMO would adapt in real-time to each player's preferences
Anish describes his vision of the ‘never-ending game’: today's MMOs are linearly scripted—if the game wants you to go from beach to forest but you prefer the ocean, it has no way to adapt. An adaptive MMO built with world models could generate an entirely new quest line in real-time for ocean lovers—suddenly spawning pirates and naval combat. He likens this to the ‘mind game’ in Ender's Game that adjusts itself to match Ender's current thoughts, suggesting future games might achieve this in reality.

item.title: Drug development's constraint isn't strict approval but invisible preclinical toxicity
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-nopriors-药物研发卡住的根源不是审批太严-而是临床前看不见毒性/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-nopriors-药物研发卡住的根源不是审批太严-而是临床前看不见毒性/
item.description: Isomorphic Labs's thesis: drug cost inflation stems from clinical failures caused by preclinical blindness to toxicity—rat testing predicts human toxicity with only ~30% accuracy.
item.content:encoded:
Isomorphic Labs's thesis: drug cost inflation stems from clinical failures caused by preclinical blindness to toxicity—rat testing predicts human toxicity with only ~30% accuracy.

The essential content clusters around the mid-episode discussion of toxicity prediction and combination therapy; the first two minutes on Max's background can be skipped.

5:23 Drug development's constraint isn't strict approval but invisible preclinical toxicity
Over decades, scientific papers increased tenfold to twentyfold and new drug modalities—antibodies, small molecules, proteins, peptides—proliferated, yet annual approvals remained flat. Development costs ballooned from millions to $1.5 billion, timelines stretched from 8–9 years to 15, and every metric worsened. Max attributes this to an industry still trapped in experience-driven trial-and-error: hypothesize a molecule, then iterate in the real world. But molecular and biological design spaces are high-dimensional and combinatorially explosive; empirical search only captures low-hanging fruit.

14:36 The goal is experimental-grade accuracy, not faster experiments
Isomorphic's north star isn't running wet experiments faster but moving drug design entirely to the computer. Max uses AlphaFold as the exemplar: structure prediction once required months or years of X-ray crystallography; if the model reaches experimental accuracy, real-world validation becomes unnecessary. Internal leaderboards mark an ‘experimental accuracy’ baseline; once crossed, wet experiments shift from ‘learning and iteration’ to ‘verification’, drastically reducing cycles in the physical world.

17:42 Clinical trials are where drug failure and costs concentrate
Unpacking the 15-year, $1.5 billion timeline: small-molecule discovery and in-vitro work occupy only 2–3 years and ~$50 million; the rest is clinical. Most failure modes—unexpected toxicity, off-target effects, or mechanisms that hit the target yet harm the body—only emerge when the drug reaches patients; animal models and in-vitro tests miss them entirely. Real gains in failure prevention come from understanding these failure modes before patient exposure.

18:46 Generate proprietary data instead of relying on public databases
Public and industry-wide data are mostly passive byproducts of historical collection, biased, and unfit for training general models demanding generalization. Isomorphic generates its own required data distributions instead of relying on existing large databases. Max noted this approach revealed ‘surprisingly impressive data scaling laws’ in model training.

20:53 Rat toxicity testing predicts human outcomes with only about 30% accuracy
Regulators mandate animal proof of safety before human use, yet toxicity frequently emerges once drugs enter patients. Max argues directly: rats aren't humans; this ‘gold standard’ predicts human clinical toxicity with about 30% accuracy—and he half-jokes that if his team's AI hit 30%, he'd ask engineers to ‘do better’. He advocates combining in-vitro experiments, AI models, and new tissue-mimicking techniques—organoids and organs-on-chip—to model human clinical toxicity directly, bypassing the five-to-six-decade-old, unreliable animal proxy.

29:21 Combination therapy fails at safety engineering, not biology
HIV and cancer treatments use cocktail approaches—tumors contain mutation spectra; single drugs prompt resistance; hitting multiple targets simultaneously prevents escape. But real-world combination therapy is rare. Max explains: existing molecules are often intrinsically toxic or damage the liver; multiple drugs generate harmful interactions. The constraint isn't biological understanding but molecular design precision—molecules lack the refinement and safety. Better-engineered, cleaner molecules unlock multi-target therapy against complex pathways.

32:17 Acceptable risk varies by disease; safety standards shouldn't be one-size-fits-all
When asked whether safety-focused regulation slows drug development, Max grants patient safety must remain central but notes risk tolerance is dynamic: COVID's pervasiveness and severity shifted social acceptance of expedited review; late-stage cancer with no alternatives and chronic low-risk disease demand vastly different risk tolerance. True progress means faster access to better treatments, not uniform safety thresholds across all disease contexts.

35:42 Extending lifespan isn't enough—drug development must also improve later-life quality
Beating cancer and heart disease still leaves aging itself—accumulated chronic problems: bone and muscle loss, post-fall immobility, compromised wellbeing and quality of life. Decades past 80 aren't inherently well-lived. Max emphasizes the industry must work both directions: treat discrete fatal diseases to extend lifespan, and tackle aging's root mechanisms to extend healthspan.

item.title: Food harbors 135,000 ‘dark matter’ molecules that science doesn't yet understand
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-thejoyofwhy-食物里还藏着13-5万种-暗物质-分子-科学还不知道它们在做什么/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-thejoyofwhy-食物里还藏着13-5万种-暗物质-分子-科学还不知道它们在做什么/
item.description: Network scientists have discovered that besides roughly 150 known nutritional components, food contains 135,000 unclassified molecules—they provide no energy but, like thousands of drugs, perform micro-level regulation inside cells.
item.content:encoded:
Network scientists have discovered that besides roughly 150 known nutritional components, food contains 135,000 unclassified molecules—they provide no energy but, like thousands of drugs, perform micro-level regulation inside cells.

One episode tracing thirty years of network science: from scale-free networks to preferential attachment to disease modules to the ‘dark matter of nutrition’—dense with information, and the latter half's medical and food cases especially worthwhile.

4:09 Everything derives meaning from connection, not from existing alone
Barabási argues science has long focused on dissecting parts while forgetting the whole—genes, neurons, and people have no meaning in isolation; function emerges only through mutual connection. Consciousness is what neurons collectively do; life is what genes and molecules collectively do; society is what people collectively do. Network science begins by mapping connections first, then asking why they exist this way, rather than studying isolated components.

14:36 Networks grow through winner-take-all mechanisms, not random chance
Traditional random graph theory assumed connections between nodes were purely determined by chance, predicting that node degrees would follow a bell curve. But actual data from the World Wide Web showed that 98% of web pages had only 1 to 5 links, while Google at the time had 800 million—a difference of several orders of magnitude. Barabási and collaborators discovered the cause: ‘preferential attachment’—when new nodes enter a network, they're more likely to connect to nodes already highly connected. This natural process creates hub nodes as networks grow, and the larger the network, the more extreme the gap between the largest hubs and smallest nodes becomes.

20:45 Random graph theory began as pure mathematics, not social reality
Strogatz explains that Erdős and Rényi originally posed the random network model to solve a pure mathematical question—using the metaphor of buttons and string: scatter buttons on a table, then randomly connect them with string. When the ratio of string to buttons reaches a critical point, picking up one button suddenly brings up a whole cluster—a discontinuous phase transition. They were pursuing the elegance of this phase transition proof, not simulating how real people make friends in society. This is the fundamental gap between the random model and actual networks.

24:57 Eighty-five percent of drugs never bind to the disease gene
Network medicine connects the ‘parts list’ from genomics with protein interactions to create a map. A disease's genes aren't randomly distributed in this network; they cluster in a specific ‘disease module’—like viewing a cell as a New York City map, psychiatric diseases clustered near Times Square, metabolic disease near Wall Street. Barabási's team found that 85% of drugs don't directly bind to the disease protein or gene itself, but instead act downstream. The disease gene usually affects too many critical processes—changing it is too risky. What matters is finding the ‘drug target’ at the right position downstream within the disease module.

32:20 One blood test saves ninety thousand dollars and six months
Take rheumatoid arthritis: the disease module consists of 100 to 200 proteins. The mainstream drug Humira can only disrupt one side of the module. If the patient's disease manifests on the other side, the drug won't work for them—explaining the medical establishment's open secret that ‘most drugs only work for 20% to 40% of patients’. Cypher, the company Barabási helped found, uses a 16-gene biomarker to predict from a single blood sample whether Humira will work for a given patient. With Humira costing $90,000 per course and conventional drug trials taking six months to determine efficacy, this test eliminates the guesswork.

37:30 Genes explain at most one-fifth of disease—environment explains the rest
Among America's ten leading causes of death, genetics explains only 10% to 20% of disease risk; the rest comes from environment—exercise, sleep, stress. The biggest single environmental factor is food. Following this logic, the team began mapping every molecule in food into a network. They discovered that conventional nutrition science recognizes only roughly 150 known components, but food actually carries 135,000 previously unclassified molecules. These molecules provide no calories and are ‘invisible’ to metabolism, earning the name ‘dark matter of nutrition’. Take polyphenols: plants can't flee, so they synthesize massive quantities of chemical compounds for defense—the onion genome is twice the size of the human genome. When polyphenols enter the body, they aren't treated as nutrients but, like thousands of drugs, bind to proteins and DNA to fine-tune cellular activity.

44:48 Barabási sees neuroscience and programmable materials as network science's next frontiers
Barabási identifies the next major breakthrough for network science: the brain. Neurons are connected permanently by synapses—a ‘physical network’ unlike the optional handshakes of social networks. This dense physical connectivity itself determines brain structure and function. Another direction builds on his early background in materials science: 3D printing now operates at molecular scale. The question becomes: if we can print any network structure, no longer constrained to regular lattices or pure randomness, what networks should we print to create entirely new materials?

item.title: Index funds are rational for everyone, but could make everyone collectively worse off in the model
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-rationalreminder-指数基金对每个人都理性-模型里却可能让所有人集体变穷/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-rationalreminder-指数基金对每个人都理性-模型里却可能让所有人集体变穷/
item.description: When diversification becomes cheap enough, money flows from individual stocks and bonds into equities, driving up share prices and depressing expected returns—everyone makes the choice optimal for themselves, yet the result might be that everyone ends up worse off. This is a tragedy of the commons.
item.content:encoded:
When diversification becomes cheap enough, money flows from individual stocks and bonds into equities, driving up share prices and depressing expected returns—everyone makes the choice optimal for themselves, yet the result might be that everyone ends up worse off. This is a tragedy of the commons.

Oxford finance professor Martin Schmalz asks a question few dare: are index funds actually good for investors as a whole? The answer is not to reject indexing, but to lower your expectations for future returns.

8:17 Index funds are rational for everyone, but make everyone worse off in the model
In Schmalz and Bill Zame's equilibrium model, index funds make diversification cheap, so more people shift money from bonds and individual stocks into equities. By supply and demand logic, increased demand raises share prices and depresses expected returns. Risk falls, but so do returns—in this simple model they perfectly offset each other, leaving every investor worse off than without index funds, despite each making the choice optimal for themselves. Schmalz stresses this is only a theoretical possibility, not a claim about reality.

17:40 Common ownership cannot be blamed solely on index funds
After examining all U.S. publicly traded companies' shareholding records over the past decade, Schmalz found that what actually drives ‘the same shareholders holding competing companies’ is often not index funds but concentrated holders like the Bill Gates family office holding multiple companies in the same industry, or Berkshire's massive stakes in multiple banks and airlines. Even when index funds are involved, common ownership arises not from the funds themselves but from concentrating all fund voting rights in a single corporate governance office that votes with one voice.

23:11 Airline ticket prices: one merger became a natural experiment
Schmalz uses BlackRock's 2009 acquisition of Barclays Global Investors as an exogenous shock—this deal clearly had nothing to do with New York-to-Boston airfares, yet unexpectedly altered U.S. airline shareholding structures. The result: on routes where common ownership increased (assuming combined holdings added up), ticket prices rose more over the following years, and this relationship was predictable in advance.

27:00 Buffett and Fink never personally push their portfolio companies to compete
Schmalz distinguishes two mechanisms: either investors call competitors to coordinate pricing, or large shareholders simply lack incentive to push their portfolio companies to compete. Richard Branson might personally get involved helping Virgin Atlantic grab market share, but no one has seen Buffett or Larry Fink do so. The issue is not ‘enabling collusion’ but ‘lacking motive to compete’—which determines what evidence to use and what policy response is appropriate.

38:18 Stripping index funds of voting rights sounds simple, but no one has modeled consequences
One frequently proposed policy is to strip large funds of voting rights. Schmalz once thought this absurd—if the 73rd-largest shareholder suddenly became the effective controller, agency problems would explode. But he later realized that once rules change, the entire shareholding structure reshuffles, and existing financial models treat shareholding structure's feedback on corporate competition and stock prices as exogenous. ‘We have almost no concept of what consequences these policies would bring.’

46:40 The character that builds wealth systematically destroys investment returns
Many family fortunes shrink dramatically within one or two generations. Schmalz attributes this not to depleted luck but to wealthy individuals lacking true diversification or bearing excessive costs. The deeper cause is the entrepreneur's personality traits—trusting handshake agreements, overconfidence, relying on intuition, craving control—which enabled their success as founders but systematically prevent them from being good investors, because investing requires due diligence, risk calibration, and deliberate decision-making rather than trust and gut feel.

56:57 Some pay fees for a fund that won't return their money to escape volatility
Schmalz uses a bungee-jumping analogy: people only truly fear falling from a cliff, and this horizon-dependent risk aversion—where fear intensifies as danger approaches—explains why volatility spikes cause panic selling, and when panic subsides people buy back in at higher prices. For these investors, paying a management fee to lock money with a fund they ‘can't call’ with ‘lock-up periods’ in place, even if it underperforms the market, beats making destructive market-timing decisions amid volatility. Cliff Asness calls the practice of allocating to illiquid private assets to avoid volatility exposure ‘volatility laundering’.

1:04:13 Two percent annual costs consume half a generation's wealth
With 7.2% annual returns, the rule of 72 makes wealth multiply 16x in 40 years—a common rule of thumb. But if annual costs add 2%, returns drop to 5.2%, and after 40 years wealth doesn't fall to 80%—it becomes only about half of 16x, or just over 7x. Schmalz notes this 2% cost easily accumulates unnoticed across asset management fees, custody fees, withholding taxes, legal and accounting fees, and private equity due diligence costs, especially for smaller family offices.

item.title: Kennedy's greatest regret: almost striking a deal with Nixon on universal healthcare in 1974
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-throughline-肯尼迪晚年最大遗憾-1974年差点和尼克松谈成全民医保/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-throughline-肯尼迪晚年最大遗憾-1974年差点和尼克松谈成全民医保/
item.description: The healthcare reform plan Nixon proposed at his lowest point during Watergate was more radical than Obamacare later, but Kennedy surrendered to pressure from allies and abandoned negotiations, calling it his greatest political regret.
item.content:encoded:
The healthcare reform plan Nixon proposed at his lowest point during Watergate was more radical than Obamacare later, but Kennedy surrendered to pressure from allies and abandoned negotiations, calling it his greatest political regret.

A single episode clearly laying out the historical fork where American healthcare reform failed, focused on the specific process of a secret negotiation, high information density in short form—28 minutes worth hearing through to the end.

6:18 Son's cancer treatment convinced Kennedy to champion universal healthcare
Kennedy's son Ted Jr. was diagnosed with bone cancer at age 12 requiring amputation. Early chemotherapy was free through clinical trials, but after the trial ended, each treatment cost $2,700 with no insurance coverage—except Kennedy himself enjoyed government insurance as a congressman. In hospital corridors, he encountered families who had mortgaged homes or faced bankruptcy unable to pay treatment costs. This experience made him embrace universal healthcare as ‘the cause of his life’.

10:30 Nixon proposed healthcare reform to deflect from Watergate
At the 1974 State of the Union address, Nixon, mired in Watergate, pivoted the conversation to healthcare, proposing a plan requiring all employers to either provide insurance or pay penalties—radical for a Republican president by today's standards. The episode notes this was not Nixon's ideological shift but a ‘president desperate to change the subject’, creating unequal motivations for the subsequent negotiations.

12:30 Kennedy saw Nixon's plan as insufficient compromise
When Nixon spoke, cameras caught Kennedy sitting unmoved—because just a year earlier, he had proposed a European-style government-led single-payer system akin to Medicare for all. Nixon's plan, in Kennedy's view, merely compromised with private insurance companies rather than constituting genuine reform.

16:36 Kennedy stunned observers by offering to work with Nixon
In April 1974, Kennedy joined the House Ways and Means Committee chairman in publicly announcing willingness to work with the Nixon administration on legislation, with media interpreting it as universal healthcare ‘a done deal’. But the decision simultaneously angered Nixon's cabinet (accusing him of ‘socialism’) and liberal allies like unions (seeing it as extending the dying Nixon's political life).

18:40 Union leaders called Kennedy a traitor to labor
Labor leaders believed Democrats would dominate the midterm elections and control both chambers, so shouldn't bargain with the departing Nixon. During negotiations, a top labor lobbyist called Kennedy a ‘traitor to labor’ to his face. Kennedy stood up, opened the door, and said ‘Then I guess you'll just have to call me a traitor’—demonstrating his determination to push forward despite pressure from allies.

19:46 Staff negotiated in secret church basement for months
Because of political sensitivity, Nixon and Kennedy's healthcare staff met secretly in a room called ‘the pub’ in the basement of St. Mark's Episcopal Church starting in June 1974, as carefully as ‘sending an envoy to the Soviet Union’, trying to find balance between government control and free competition. Negotiations continued through July.

22:02 Negotiations continued even as Watergate hearings intensified
Even as impeachment hearings unfolded in the House and White House tapes were turned over to prosecutors, church basement negotiations continued discussing technical details like payroll taxes and insurance rules, because participants still saw this ‘historic window’ as open. On July 8, 1974—just one month before Nixon resigned—his health secretary still told Kennedy ‘reaching agreement is possible’.

23:06 Kennedy quietly walked away from the historic opportunity
After assessing how much he had compromised and how strongly allies had backlashed, Kennedy told his staff ‘They're prepared to crucify me’, then arranged no further meetings or calls. The negotiations simply faded away. A month later Nixon resigned and the healthcare plan disappeared entirely, ‘just like that’.

item.title: $500 Million Ammo Factory Delivered Nothing in Two Years, Military Never Asked for a Penny Back
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-papertrail-5亿美元炮弹新厂两年颗粒无收-军方却从不索回一分钱/

item.description: General Dynamics' Turkish-sourced equipment produced not a single compliant shell in two years. After halting two production lines, the military kept paying progress installments, demanded no compensation, terminated no contract, and instead awarded the company new deals.
item.content:encoded:
General Dynamics' Turkish-sourced equipment produced not a single compliant shell in two years. After halting two production lines, the military kept paying progress installments, demanded no compensation, terminated no contract, and instead awarded the company new deals.

A specific factory case that demonstrates how military-industrial outsourcing loses control when politicians demand immediate results. The story's dense operational detail concentrates in the back half; the opening drags somewhat.

6:20 Only one supplier exists; the military has no bargaining power
The U.S. was producing 14,000 shells monthly and needed 100,000; General Dynamics was the only company capable of manufacturing this artillery shell casing. The reporter explains this reflects a structural reality of the entire defense industry: massive consolidation has left suppliers few and nearly monopolistic, while the customer is just the Pentagon. Both parties are locked in deep mutual dependence—a General Dynamics failure would be catastrophic for the Pentagon, leaving the military with no choice but to keep awarding contracts to the same company.

8:24 Unproven technology was approved as the solution anyway
General Dynamics did not replicate the century-old methodology from existing plants. Instead, it adopted a completely new ‘flow forming’ system from Turkish company Repcon, claimed to be flexible enough to adjust like clay pottery for different shell calibers. Yet Repcon had never produced this specific shell type with this machine anywhere, and it refused to let the military observe a successful demonstration, citing protection of other customers' privacy. These were known red flags on the table before approval—and the contract was greenlit anyway.

10:24 Work started before contract details were negotiated
2022 legislation allowed the Pentagon to skip competitive bidding and select suppliers directly. The military used ‘undefinitized contracting action’—companies could start working while contract specifics were hammered out later. A defense industry executive described it as building the plane while flying it. Internal military objections existed, but pressure to move fast cascaded from the White House through the Pentagon to the military command. With $500 million being rounding error in a trillion-dollar budget, the risk was deemed an acceptable cost.

13:36 Robots drenched in flammable oil caught fire regularly
From day one, workers discovered the entire production line was systematically broken. Enormous robotic arms would suddenly thrash, smashing other equipment, and they were constantly sprayed with flammable lubricant. Workers stopped being surprised when robots caught fire—they privately called that period ‘the summer of burning robots.’ Stamping machine components seized; workers had to pound them with sledgehammers each night. A supposedly precision piece of expensive equipment was maintained by a rotating crew swinging sledges.

15:43 The factory building itself appeared to be sinking
The facility's most basic infrastructure—conveyor belts, automated carts—failed constantly. The workshop ran year-round above 100 degrees Fahrenheit. More disturbing was the building itself: cracks appeared in walls, daylight showed through window frames, doors dragged on the floor and wouldn't open. Multiple workers eventually realized the factory's foundation was shifting, even subsiding, as if the earth itself was pulling the malfunctioning plant down.

19:52 The core machine cracked shells; mutual suspicion deepened
The much-hyped flow forming machine regularly fractured shells into scrap. Only Repcon's Turkish operators could touch it; they were secretive with General Dynamics' workers, who could only infer problems from metal shavings on the floor. More unsettling: General Dynamics workers discovered the machine was moving on its own—Repcon was controlling it remotely from Turkey. General Dynamics' response was to physically disable remote access. Suspicion and rumors of ‘sabotage’ spread through the plant, though the reporter found no evidence of actual sabotage.

22:56 Leadership's public story diverged completely from factory reality
While the factory was producing nothing and workers were hiding chairs to prevent sleeping, General Dynamics' CEO told investors in an earnings call that the facility was ‘rapidly ramping ammunition production.’ Military procurement officials publicly said delays were ‘measured in weeks, not months or years.’ Not until June 2025, when industry media exposed internal military correspondence threatening contract termination, did the public learn that the military had long known the plant was a disaster—they just had not said so.

27:10 After shutdown, the military kept paying without accountability
In August 2025, the military halted two of three production lines—lines that had not produced a single usable shell. That December, the military still paid General Dynamics over $20 million in progress installments. The final settlement: General Dynamics would spend $200 million to fix equipment, trivial for a company with $50 billion prior-year revenue. The military demanded no repayment of the initial $500 million. The unit that established this facility later received $2.5 billion in new contracts. Former military officials acknowledge the structural bind: neither party could afford to let the other fail.

item.title: Liquidating a whale's position 22 times by hand: leverage is just fourth-grade division
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-complexsys-手动清算一个巨鲸的仓位22次-杠杆率只是四年级除法/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-complexsys-手动清算一个巨鲸的仓位22次-杠杆率只是四年级除法/
item.description: During the FTX collapse, a whale account on Solend became insolvent as the liquidation system failed. The author manually liquidated it 22 times—doing what the liquidation robots should have done—and earned about 50% in returns.
item.content:encoded:
During the FTX collapse, a whale account on Solend became insolvent as the liquidation system failed. The author manually liquidated it 22 times—doing what the liquidation robots should have done—and earned about 50% in returns.

The first half explains leverage with extreme clarity—add one and take the reciprocal, and you can learn it in thirty seconds. The second half is a rare firsthand record of DeFi liquidations, worth listening to in full.

1:06 Mental math for leverage: add one and take the reciprocal
The author presents a formula you can calculate in your head: add one to the leverage ratio and take its reciprocal—that's how much the asset value has to fall before equity reaches zero. A 10:1 leveraged company only needs its assets to drop about one-ninth (9.09%) to wipe out equity entirely. This reduces leverage from something mystical to fourth-grade division, and it's fundamental to understanding the whale story that follows.

3:55 Brokers manage your leverage for their benefit, not yours
Brokers are willing to lend you money to increase leverage on stock purchases because it's a high-engagement feature that attracts customers. But once the stock price falls and your leverage ratio climbs, the broker issues a margin call requiring you to reduce positions or add funds. The author emphasizes that if brokers don't quickly reduce your leverage, the bad debt likely won't be recovered—especially from retail traders, whose other finances are usually equally stressed when an account goes underwater.

3:55 Paying down debt and depositing savings have different effects
Depositing the same $400 produces different outcomes: if paid as cash toward a loan, leverage drops to 0.6:1, well below the 1:1 baseline; if deposited as stock collateral, it only returns to 1:1. The difference is that stock collateral introduces new risk exposure, while debt repayment purely reduces risk. This explains why regulators and brokers prefer to demand cash rather than collateral when deleveraging customers.

12:13 A whale account goes insolvent, and the liquidation robots all malfunction
The FTX collapse triggered a SOL price crash. The Solend protocol was designed so liquidation robots would take the whale's collateral at a 5% discount to execute deleveraging. But the whale's position was far too large for the robots' risk appetite; they could only nibble at it gradually, and during the SOL crash, many robots found no attractive liquidity and simply couldn't operate. The whale account slid from conservative leverage all the way to insolvency.

12:13 The protocol raises the SOL deposit rate to 2600% and still can't get takers
Other users had borrowed the whale's SOL to short it, leaving the protocol with only USDC claims against the whale and no actual SOL to disburse. The Solend team manually raised the SOL deposit APY to 2400%-2600%, trying to attract more SOL deposits, but in the general market panic, the rate wasn't enough. Many robots simply powered down, leaving the operators to sleep with the concern that the protocol's hole might expand.

12:13 A mind-numbingly boring game where 70% of operations crash
The author didn't have time to code a liquidation robot, so they became one: deposit some USDC, wait for more SOL to flow in at the high rate, manually liquidate part of the whale's debt, and swap the discounted SOL back to USDC, then repeat. The program crashed about 70% of the time; operations that should have taken seconds took 3 to 12 minutes, until people in other time zones woke up and restarted the bots, and then the AI "stole" their clicking work.

21:31 A 5% discount repeated 22 times isn't triple the returns
The naive calculation says 1.05^22 should approach 3x the capital, but after slippage and fees taken by the game's designer, actual returns were about 50%. The author compares the experience to playing poker for two hours with similar returns but possibly higher risk, and says they'd rather play Dyson Sphere Program or Factorio next time.

item.title: The biggest loophole in NVIDIA's China chip controls: not selling chips, but renting them to you
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-oddlots-nvidia对华芯片管控的最大漏洞-不卖芯片-租给你用/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-oddlots-nvidia对华芯片管控的最大漏洞-不卖芯片-租给你用/
item.description: Megaspeed spent $4.6 billion on NVIDIA chips to sublease to Alibaba, and remote access breaks no law; after NVIDIA's own audit, 50,000 chips remain unaccounted for, some of them the most advanced Blackwell.
item.content:encoded:
Megaspeed spent $4.6 billion on NVIDIA chips to sublease to Alibaba, and remote access breaks no law; after NVIDIA's own audit, 50,000 chips remain unaccounted for, some of them the most advanced Blackwell.

A single listen to understand the technical details of the Megaspeed scandal, how remote access as a legal loophole works, and the role NVIDIA played in law enforcement investigation—high information density, no filler.

4:07 Megaspeed assembled $4.6 billion in NVIDIA chips through an intricate shell company structure
Megaspeed is Southeast Asia's largest NVIDIA chip buyer and Alibaba's primary compute supplier. It was spun off from a Chinese gaming company, went through a BVI shell company, registered in Singapore, and became an official NVIDIA partner four days later. The company has been under investigation by the US and Singapore for at least a year. According to reporter Mackenzie Hawkins, it is 100% owned by Singaporeans, but its structure is essentially that of a shell company, and the source of its funding remains an unresolved question.

15:37 After its own audit, NVIDIA still cannot account for 50,000 chips
At the US government's request, NVIDIA tallied the chips Megaspeed had received across three countries, eight companies, and over a dozen data centers. In November 2024, it stated publicly that ‘all shipments to our partners are where they should be.’ But after cross-checking with trade records from Malaysia and Indonesia, the reporter found roughly 50,000 chips unaccounted for, most of them NVIDIA's then-best hardware, Blackwell. NVIDIA later found another batch of previously undisclosed warehouses but has consistently refused to confirm the exact numbers. In December it only vaguely said it had found ‘essentially all’ of the chips, promising further audits—but when the reporter pressed for details more than a dozen times afterward, NVIDIA provided no answers.

18:44 Megaspeed presented a Shanghai project as an unnamed third country data center to investors
Megaspeed's website lists three data centers, but its 2024 pitch to investors described five, spanning three countries, one located in ‘an unnamed third country’—yet the rendering shown was for a Shanghai project under construction. This was precisely where Megaspeed's ‘corporate twin’ company in China was hiring engineers to use restricted NVIDIA hardware, and the investors behind it have long-standing business dealings with Alice (the executive caught up in Jensen Huang's affair). The company has offered no explanation.

28:02 Renting NVIDIA chips to Chinese AI companies is legal in nine of ten cases
So long as the data center sits in Southeast Asia, and you remotely rent computing power to cutting-edge Chinese AI companies—even for training the most advanced open-source models—it is legal in the overwhelming majority of cases. The one exception is knowing that the compute will be used by a foreign adversary's military or intelligence service. In its final days, the Biden administration issued a global restriction scheme called the AI diffusion rule in an attempt to close this loophole, originally set to take effect in May 2025, but the Trump administration has not enforced it. Morgan Stanley and others call it a ‘loophole in export controls,’ but legally speaking, it is merely the US government's own policy choice, not a loophole.

32:09 NVIDIA's general counsel called export control enforcement directly about the investigation
NVIDIA's general counsel Tim Teeter called the head of BIS, the export control enforcement agency, directly in late summer last year, asking whether they had been involved in the investigation into Alice's detention in Singapore—NVIDIA claimed Teeter didn't know at the time that she was Jensen Huang's extramarital partner. Thereafter, if investigators wanted information from NVIDIA, they had to first get approval from or route it through Jeffrey Kessler, a special privilege no other major tech company has enjoyed. This weakened the agency's investigative capability, and ultimately BIS handed the case to DOJ, the Department of Justice.

38:21 DeepSeek ordered 160,000 Huawei chips but must wait over a year for delivery
DeepSeek placed a large order for 160,000 of Huawei's best AI chips, the 950DT, for the next-generation hyperscale compute cluster it is building in Inner Mongolia—though the US government believes DeepSeek installed NVIDIA's Blackwell chips at this same location. Huawei simply does not have the capacity to deliver this order within a year, and DeepSeek has even lobbied China's government to press Huawei to accelerate delivery. The 950DT was designed by Huawei for training; DeepSeek plans to use it for inference first, not training.

41:23 Huawei exported its best chips to Egypt using its old telecom playbook
Huawei bid on a tender with Egypt's government to provide AI computing power to Egyptian defense-related enterprises—a small volume, about 2,000 chips, yet Huawei deployed its best hardware. With capacity so tight, every chip exported has to be squeezed out of domestic allocation. After spotting this, the US government hastily convened a consortium of American companies to counter-bid, since almost no one has previously treated Egypt as a key market. This is seen as the same playbook Huawei used to dominate 3G and 4G telecom equipment globally, and the US is trying to prevent history from repeating.

item.title: Measles virus: thirty years unchanged because simultaneous protein mutations are mathematically impossible
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-twiv-麻疹病毒三十年不变异-多突变同时发生在数学上不可能/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-twiv-麻疹病毒三十年不变异-多突变同时发生在数学上不可能/
item.description: Measles is an RNA virus but mutates almost never, because vaccine escape requires multiple mutations in F and H proteins simultaneously—probability makes this nearly impossible—which is why the same vaccine works for decades.
item.content:encoded:
Measles is an RNA virus but mutates almost never, because vaccine escape requires multiple mutations in F and H proteins simultaneously—probability makes this nearly impossible—which is why the same vaccine works for decades.

First half: a CDC veteran reviews 40 years of measles control and assesses America's imminent loss of elimination status. Second half: two novel laboratory findings (mitochondrial targeting, bulk cell extrusion). Dense with information but leisurely pace—suitable for faster playback.

10:27 The 1990s outbreak was not caused by viral mutation
CDC suspected antigenic drift—the team's flu background made them habitually think in terms of antigenic shift. But sequencing and antigen analysis showed the virus itself hadn't changed significantly. The real cause was collapsing vaccination rates: inner-city coverage fell below 50%. When infectious disease outbreaks occur, don't presume viral mutation; check vaccination coverage first.

12:44 Five naming systems for one virus—unified only in 1997
Different labs used five or six naming systems for the same sequences—some called them genotypes one, two, three; others used A, B, C—all describing the same virus. At WHO level, CDC organized a meeting that unified measles genotyping strategy in 1997: sequencing the high-variability region of N protein's carboxyl terminus, 450 nucleotides. This was a significant technical burden for many labs at the time.

15:58 Sub-Saharan Africa has most cases but almost no sequences in the database
The global sequencing database holds thousands of sequences from the Americas, Western Europe, even parts of the Western Pacific. Yet most measles infections actually occur in sub-Saharan Africa, where the database contains only a handful. The bottleneck isn't lab capacity but field sampling and transport—pharyngeal swabs, proper conditions. Both are challenges in low-income settings.

24:29 The 6-versus-11 hospitalization gap proves measles is no mild disease
Current measles hospitalization is about 6%, but historical average runs 11-12%, meaning roughly one in ten infected children may require ICU care—even from complications like dehydration alone. This number rebuts claims measles is mild. But speakers acknowledged that past vaccine-safety rhetoric may no longer persuade today's vaccine-hesitant populations.

25:33 America will probably lose measles elimination status
Kindergarten vaccination coverage has dropped to about 92%—sounds acceptable, but national averages mask counties below 80%. The Pan American Health Organization's regional verification committee meets in November to assess: three consecutive years without sustained transmission required. Brazil, Venezuela, and the UK have lost and regained elimination status—it's reversible, but regaining it demands the same strict standards.

37:15 One stretch of N protein targets itself to mitochondria—reason unknown
A graduate student found that the N protein C-terminal sequence alone, fused to GFP, gets directed into mitochondria, while the full N protein in cells goes to the nucleus—implying N protein contains conflicting targeting signals. In infected cells, mitochondria break down, mitochondrial DNA releases into cytoplasm and activates cGAS, upregulating interferon-stimulated genes. Yet surprisingly, interferon itself doesn't markedly increase. This contradiction remains unexplained.

42:26 Measles might exit respiratory epithelium by bulk cell shedding not budding
Measles enters respiratory epithelium via the basolateral route and spreads between cells, then entire infected zones slough off the epithelium—involving hundreds to thousands of cells at once. This massive cell extrusion hasn't been observed with any other viral infection. Researchers hypothesize that infected cell clusters plus free virus together may partly explain why measles spreads more readily than other respiratory viruses.

49:41 Canine distemper virus in human epithelial cells triggers no infection
Canine distemper virus can't infect human respiratory epithelium and shows no cell cluster shedding. But in ferret respiratory epithelium, infected zones slough off identically. This suggests bulk cell extrusion is probably a host-virus-specific interaction, not a universal trait of measles viruses.

item.title: The Jars Are Stone, but the Bones Are from 1000 CE
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-ancients-老挝石缸之谜-石器摆在那-人骨却是公元1000年的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-ancients-老挝石缸之谜-石器摆在那-人骨却是公元1000年的/
item.description: The jars themselves can't be radiocarbon-dated, but human bones, tooth ablation, and dates clustering around 1000 CE both inside and outside the jars suggest this stone-jar mortuary tradition persisted long after the Iron Age.
item.content:encoded:
The jars themselves can't be radiocarbon-dated, but human bones, tooth ablation, and dates clustering around 1000 CE both inside and outside the jars suggest this stone-jar mortuary tradition persisted long after the Iron Age.

Two leading archaeologists discuss an as-yet-unpublished excavation at Site 75 with high information density, suited to anyone interested in Southeast Asian archaeology or ancient mortuary practices.

4:05 Stone jars can't be dated; the bones inside belong to 1000 CE
Stone jars are stone—not organic material—so radiocarbon-dating is impossible. Early scholar Madeleine Colani proposed in the 1920s–30s that they belonged to the Iron Age, between 100 BCE and 500 CE, a view that persisted. But human remains and organic materials excavated around Sites 1 and 75 in recent years have yielded dates clustering around 1000 CE, hundreds of years later. Since the jars themselves cannot be dated, researchers must rely on indirect inference from surrounding deposits and bones. This gap is why the debate persists.

8:16 The Plain of Jars is not a plain but about 127 scattered sites across mountains
Plain of Jars misleadingly suggests a single valley. It actually refers to a vast region spanning northern Laos into Vietnam and northern Myanmar, with about 127 known sites spread across hundreds of kilometers. Each site receives a number—Site 1, Site 2, Site 3—assigned in discovery order. Site 1 is the largest, most famous, and the only major tourist attraction, but most others lie hidden in remote mountains. Some sites hold one jar; others as many as 400 at a single location.

10:18 Laos suffered the heaviest bombing per capita; archaeologists must clear ordnance first
Xinhuang Province, where the stone jars stand, endured massive bombing during the Secret War of the 1960s–70s, when the U.S. conducted covert raids against North Vietnamese supply lines. Laos has been more heavily bombed per capita and by total tonnage than anywhere on Earth. Before excavation, archaeologists must hire specialized UXO clearance teams to sweep each site. At Site 75, nearby hillsides still bear massive bomb craters, and the main jar's wall damage likely came from an explosion.

13:22 Bombs have become everyday objects here—house pillars, planters, cutlery—still injuring children
In the stone-jar region, bombs are not historical artifacts but still-present objects in daily use, still causing injuries. Locals stand bomb casings upright as house-foundation pillars, repurpose them as planters, and melt the metal to make spoons and jewelry. The region has many bomb-injured residents. Cluster munitions, round and toy-like, kill and wound children with particular frequency. War's legacy is not a history-book entry but lived daily risk.

20:34 Scholars agree jars served burial purposes; the actual methods vary entirely site to site
Researchers broadly accept that stone jars relate to mortuary practice, yet the specific methods differ radically. Colani found cremated bones inside jars at Site 1, suggesting cremation occurred there. Others have found secondary-burial bones stacked on the ground near jars, pottery burials, and one primary interment. At Site 75, roughly 40 individuals were deposited in a single jar with no cremation. Different sites show completely different mortuary methods. Only about 12% of known sites have been excavated or surveyed, so unified conclusions seem unlikely. Burial practice appears highly localized, perhaps even family- or clan-specific.

30:17 One jar held forty people—but only scattered fragments, not complete skeletons
Site 75's largest jar held remains attributable to roughly 40 individuals, but not 40 complete skeletons—rather scattered bone fragments and teeth, many poorly preserved. This indicates secondary burial: the body decomposed or was defleshed elsewhere, bones were collected later, then deposited in the jar, unlike primary burial where the body goes directly underground. The remains range from roughly 18 months old to adults, some teeth show ablation marks, and the age span of the bones suggests roughly 200 years, implying the jar saw reuse across multiple generations by the same family or group.

41:36 Twenty glass beads prove this society traded with South Asia and Sassanid Persia
Analysis of 20 glass beads from Site 75 shows they match characteristics of South Asian production between the 1st millennium BCE and the 11th century CE, with one possibly from the Sassanid Empire. This demolishes the old image of jar culture as isolated and closed. These people clearly participated in broader trade networks. The beads, along with iron tools (a small knife) and pottery vessels left as grave goods, suggest this location lay on trade routes—a hypothesis Colani first advanced.

46:58 The jars were carved on-site from raw stone, not shaped at a quarry and hauled upslope
Test pits beside Site 75 show stratigraphy revealing how the jars were installed: people raised and leveled the natural slope to create a platform, positioned the stone there, then wedged large shale or slate blocks underneath to prevent rocking. Crucially, the jars are made of conglomerate—naturally cemented small stones—and carving sheds chips that accumulate at the base. These chips lie exactly where they should if the jars were carved on-site from raw stone, not shaped at a quarry and hauled whole upslope.

item.content:encoded:
Rasputin warned the tsar against entering World War I—one of his rare correct judgments—but the tsar never heeded him on military matters. Yet on personnel appointments, the tsar gave the empress and Rasputin a free hand, ultimately destroying the empire's entire administrative system.

This episode is not sensationalist history but uses one concrete figure to explain why autocracy rots from within. Information-dense; worth hearing in full.

6:27 Defeat in the Russo-Japanese War forced the tsar to accept a power-limiting constitution
Rasputin's rise had deep roots: the tsar's humiliating defeat in the Russo-Japanese War—land forces defeated, the Far Eastern fleet annihilated, and the Baltic fleet sent to circumnavigate the globe for revenge only to be destroyed en route. All responsibility fell on the tsar. By late 1905, he was forced to accept a constitution that curtailed the Romanov autocracy. It was amid this humiliation and turmoil that the imperial family's obsession with mysticism and shamanic figures reached its height, paving the way for Rasputin.

15:50 The tsarevich's hemophilia crisis gave the empress near-absolute power
The heir apparent, Alexei, had hemophilia. During a hunting trip to Spala in Poland, an attack brought him to the brink of death; doctors prepared the parents for their child's passing. Rasputin, from elsewhere, merely phoned to say ‘the child will be fine’—and the boy recovered. From that moment, Rasputin held nearly absolute control over the empress. Everyone around the royal family watched helplessly as decision-making power fell into the hands of this Siberian.

20:00 Rasputin's warning against entering the war was one of his rare correct calls
Rasputin opposed Russia entering the First World War and even wrote letters to the tsar warning it would be a complete disaster, possibly ending the entire autocracy itself. Events proved him entirely correct. Yet the tsar never accepted Rasputin's advice on military matters—the one counsel he should have heeded was precisely the one he ignored.

27:25 The empress convinced the tsar to take personal command of the military
In 1915, the empress—working in concert with Rasputin—convinced the tsar that his cousin Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolayevich was plotting a coup. She pressured him to assume personal command of the Russian army and move to Stavka, the highest command post. Britain, France, allied governments, and virtually all ministers (except the prime minister) warned it would be catastrophic. The tsar ignored them. The result was one of the largest retreats in Russian history: vast territories in Poland and Belarus were abandoned. From then on, every military defeat bore the tsar's name.

29:32 Ministers rotated constantly and no one could truly control any department
After the tsar left the capital, the empress, under Rasputin's influence, constantly replaced ministers and governors, retaining only those who obeyed her and Rasputin absolutely. This came to be called ‘leapfrogging of ministers’. The result: no minister had a real opportunity to master his own department or manage his subordinates' civil service systems. The entire state machinery ground to a halt.

38:08 Killing Rasputin became a farce marred by failure after failure
Three right-wing nobles, led by Prince Yusupov, conspired to assassinate Rasputin to ‘save Russia’—but bungled it into absurdity. Cyanide-laced Madeira wine and poisoned cakes failed; the sugar in the pastries neutralized the toxin. After being shot, he still tried to escape the courtyard. Only a bullet to the back finally killed him. The man known for predicting the future could not foresee his own death.

40:15 Killing Rasputin did not halt the monarchy's slide toward collapse
The conspirators expected that removing Rasputin would shatter the empress's psyche, even force the tsar to abdicate and reinstall Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolayevich as commander. Instead, the opposite happened: the royal family withdrew further into isolation and ceased listening to any other Romanov relatives. The situation simply continued its descent toward revolution—and the new interior minister they appointed afterward proved even more catastrophic than the ministers Rasputin had influenced.

41:15 Frozen trains in the wrong places starved the capital and toppled the tsar
Protopopov, an interior minister elevated through Rasputin's influence, suffered from tertiary syphilis-induced psychosis—yet was put in charge of transportation. In January and February 1917, because he sent trains to the wrong depots, they froze solid in the harsh winter and became unusable. The capital did not lack grain; it lacked the ability to move grain into the city. This human-caused food shortage set hungry crowds in motion and finally brought down the tsar.

item.title: Lawrence betrayed not the Arabs, but the British Empire he had sworn to serve
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-empirehist-劳伦斯真正背叛的不是阿拉伯人-而是自己效忠的大英帝国/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-empirehist-劳伦斯真正背叛的不是阿拉伯人-而是自己效忠的大英帝国/
item.description: After learning early of the secret pact dividing the Arab world between Britain and France, British intelligence officer Lawrence did not remain loyal to the Empire—instead, he told Faisal, ‘Don't trust my government's promises,’ and chose his side first.
item.content:encoded:
After learning early of the secret pact dividing the Arab world between Britain and France, British intelligence officer Lawrence did not remain loyal to the Empire—instead, he told Faisal, ‘Don't trust my government's promises,’ and chose his side first.

Debunk the film's myth of Lawrence single-handedly seizing Aqaba, and reveal the true story woven from gold, intelligence, and personal choice.

4:07 Gallipoli and Kut destroyed Lawrence's faith in British military command
He might have landed at Alexandretta, struck south into Anatolia along the railways and roads—but instead the Army chose Gallipoli, the Ottoman Empire's most difficult beachhead. The Turks fortified it completely; the landing became catastrophic. At the Siege of Kut, rescue forces found a fortress empty at dawn and attacked the same position four hours later, throwing away hundreds of lives. Sent as negotiator to seek Turkish surrender terms, Lawrence concluded that British commanders were simply incompetent.

8:13 The uprising had already stalled four months before Lawrence arrived
The film begins with Lawrence's entrance, but Sharif Hussein fired the first shot four months earlier. He took Mecca and parts of the coast, then movement stopped. North to Greater Syria: almost nothing. By the standards of the time, the uprising deserved a D. The negotiations between McMahon and Hussein that sparked it had nothing to do with Lawrence—that's pure cinema invention.

11:22 One intelligence report on Faisal turned Lawrence into a consequential figure
Lawrence traveled south with Ronald Storls to meet Hussein's four sons. Abdullah: hostile from the start. Zaid: too young. Ali: too purely religious, not a soldier. Then came Faisal—tall, schooled in Istanbul, composed, charismatic—and Lawrence thought ‘that's him’. Back in Cairo, he filed an intelligence report naming Faisal the uprising's true leader. The report was brilliantly written, and it reshaped Lawrence's standing in Cairo and London alike.

13:26 Gold shipped by the Royal Navy was the true fuel of the uprising
The Arab revolt depended on British money from its inception: pound gold coins shipped in bulk across the Red Sea by the Royal Navy. Once Lawrence entered the system, he became chief liaison—deciding who got paid and how much. These sums were trivial next to Western Front expenses, but in Arabia armies ran on cash and grain; whoever controlled the purse held real power.

16:31 Starving the Medina garrison was far more effective than trying to assault it
Medina held fifteen thousand Turkish troops. London discussed how to storm and capture it. Lawrence argued: leave it alone. Keep the Hejaz Railway—the lifeline—open but don't breach it entirely, and the garrison stays pinned, afraid to break out. Frontal assault would cost blood; letting the enemy defeat itself works better. This doctrine—‘shapeless as vapor, always on the move’—became his central method for commanding the Arab forces.

19:33 Lawrence disclosed the secret partition treaty to Faisal before anyone else learned it
From the intelligence world, Lawrence learned of the Sykes-Picot pact early: Britain and France carving up the Arab territories. It made him sick. But he did not guard the secret. He told Faisal: don't believe what your government promises. If you want independence, you will have to seize it yourselves. After that, Faisal became noticeably harder, his distrust of the British sharpened, and Arab tactics changed course. Scott calls it genuine betrayal—of a kind.

32:11 Aqaba fell through Turkish blunders, not through Lawrence's legendary cavalry charge
The film shows Lawrence leading a mounted assault and seizing Aqaba. Reality: Turkish guns pointed at the sea, leaving their rear unguarded—like Singapore in 1942, but reversed. Real fighting lasted one brief clash on the slope below. Aqaba itself nearly surrendered without contest: the Turks saw Arab numbers and chose to retreat. Lawrence rode a camel in; partway there it took fire and collapsed. He walked the final distance into Aqaba on foot, the camel's corpse behind him.

36:19 Bolsheviks and Balfour exposed the partition treaty—Arabs learned they'd been betrayed twice
In four weeks of November 1917: the Bolsheviks took power, opened the Tsar's archives, and released Sykes-Picot to the world. Then came the Balfour Declaration, promising British backing for a Jewish homeland in Palestine—the same territory, pledged to two different peoples. Faisal and Hussein were shocked and felt sold out. One month before, Lawrence had confessed to a friend, George Lloyd: he no longer fought for His Majesty's Government, but for Hussein and the Arab people. A witness's account, not Lawrence's own later embellishment.

item.title: Russia lifted its siege, but Britain and France fabricated a pretext to invade Crimea
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-12-restishistory-俄军已主动撤围-英法却现编了一个入侵克里米亚的理由/
